MR. PRUD'HOMME-COMMENT BY MEMBER FOR YORK SOUTH RESPECTING TRIP TO ARAB COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take the first opportunity given to me to rise on a question of privilege of which I have given you notice pursuant to Standing Orders.
It relates to comments made by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) and reported in the Ottawa Citizen of January 23, 1970; they deal with an invitation from the United Arab Republic to attend a peace conference to be held in the Middle East and to visit the Arab countries.
This is a matter interesting all members of Parliament who are occasionally invited by countries-friendly, neutral or former enemy countries-with which we have friendly relations.
Besides, many other members have accompanied me on that journey and I would not want to give here a list of the invitations I have accepted, along with members of the New Democratic party, to go to Washington or elsewhere.
I strongly protest against the innuendos of such a statement because it could cast doubts on my objectivity with respect to that tragic conflict.
As a matter of fact, I rose in the past against the spreading of hate propaganda against the Jews as is shown in the official report of the House of Commons' debates of June 1 and 14, 1967, at pages 824 and 1514.
I raise a strong protest against such insinuations which could make any invitation any member of Parliament could receive in future subject to criticism. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege is so justified that I am not requesting you to refer it to the Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PRUD'HOMME-COMMENT BY MEMBER FOR YORK SOUTH RESPECTING TRIP TO ARAB COUNTRIES
speechtext:
The hon. member has given me notice of the question of privilege he intended to raise, in accordance with Standing Orders. After studying the question and after hearing the hon. member's remarks, I would doubt that a question of privilege is in order when all the hon. member has to complain about is that another member suggests that a given action is not proper. I believe it is a matter of translation. We use the word "con-venable" whereas the word the hon. member for York South used in English is more specific.

I believe the complaint of the hon. member is that another hon. member has questioned the propriety of a certain action. I would think that this is a rather mild reference to the action of an hon. member and I fail to see how a question of privilege could be raised on this basis.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
I have to add the circumstance that the matter was raised outside the House, not in the chamber, and for this reason I do not think there would be a question of privilege. As a third consideration, no motion having been moved the matter cannot be referred to a committee and no further action can be taken by the House.

Under the circumstances, I must render the decision that there is no ground for the question of privilege and that this matter cannot be considered further.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the ground ol urgent and pressing necessity I ask the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion based on the following facts.
Following the announcement by the United States authorities on February 6, it is now certain that the phase-down of the Argentia naval base will leave more than 350 men unemployed on March 20, without alternative employment. These men have up to 27 years employment at the Argentia base. They are being let out on 30 days notice and with inadequate severance allowance or pension. These men are declared redundant in a province where the unemployment rate is close to 20 per cent. My motion reads as follows:
That the government take immediate measures to counteract the economic and social disaster which has struck the people of the Argentia community due to the phase-down of the Argentia naval base.

that Bill C-186, to establish a commission for the reform of the laws of Canada be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the government is fulfilling a commitment which I made when I participated in a convocation at the Osgoode Law School in October, 1968, that within 18 months we would introduce a bill to establish a law reform commission for Canada.

In the interval, I have had the opportunity of discussing the nature of the proposed commission with several jurisdictions. This is the first time, to my knowledge, that there will exist in the legal world a law commission relating to the federal laws of a federal state. I had the opportunity last October of holding conversations on three separate occasions in London with the chairman of the English and Welsh Law Reform Commission, Sir Leslie Scarman, who a year earlier had been the guest of the Canadian Bar Association at its annual convention. He is now, and has been since its inception, the chairman of the Law Reform Commission in England. We were able to discuss the statutory framework of such a commission, the way in which it worked, its relationship to parliament, to the bench, the bar and the legal profession generally, as well as to the public. At the same time I had the opportunity of discussing the subject with Lord Kilbrandon, who is the chairman of the Scottish Law Reform Commission which has responsibility for Law reform in the Scottish system of law and jurisprudence. It is noteworthy that in the United Kingdom they should have decided to set up two separate law reform commissions for two separate systems of law. We, in Canada, have decided upon a single commission which will embrace within its purview two systems of law-the system of Anglo-American jurisprudence which obtains in nine of the ten provinces, and the civil law system which is practised in the province of Quebec and which derives from the Napoleonic Code and the French jurisprudence. We have also held discussions with members of the Ontario Law Reform Commission and reviewed the practice of the New York State Law Reform Commission.
The purpose of the bill before us is to establish a law reform commission in Canada. The commission will consist of a chairman and vice-chairman, two other full-time members and two part-time members. All appointments would be for a term not exceeding seven years for full-time members and not exceeding three years for part-time members. This would permit the commission to be renewed on a continuing basis. What we are attempting to institute here is a relatively small commission made up of personnel reflecting the priorities of law reform as they arise from time to time. I do not anticipate that the commission will provide a carrer. What we are looking for are men and women whose particular expertise and competence will
February 23, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill
reflect the priorities of law reform in the next five to seven years; as these priorities are changed, the personnel of the commission will be rotated, and new men and women will be commissioned to meet the responsibilities and priorities of the next period of reform.
I said I wanted the best years of their lives-men and women, of legal competence primarily-though members could be drawn from other disciplines if that could be arranged to meet the priorities of law reform. At least four members of the commission must be from the legal profession, either barristers or judges, but, as I have said, there is room on the commission for others outside those professions. At least two members of the commission, including either the chairman or the vice-chairman, must represent and reflect the civil law system in Quebec.
The commission would have a permanent staff appointed under the Public Service Employment Act, and it would have power to contract out work for specific projects. It follows that the necessary specialized expertise would be available to it. We realize it would be impossible to incorporate within such a compact commission as is proposed, all the expertise, specialized legal knowledge and familiarity with allied disciplines necessary. So the commission will be empowered to employ on a relatively short-term basis, experts in particular fields under review.
The commission will enjoy a substantial degree of independence. For example, it will be able to receive proposals for law reform from any person; and it will have power to initiate and carry out such studies as it deems necessary. However, it will be required to submit its program to the Attorney General of Canada, and the Attorney General, or the Minister of Justice, will have authority to insert any program for reform into the commission's program for study, should he deem it in the interest of Canada, and the commission will be bound to give such a program special priority when required. This provision has been inserted so as to ensure that the research program and undertakings of the commission will be' related to the priorities in law reform as they appear relevant from time to time, having regard to the priorities of the people as reflected by the debates in Parliament and so on. It is essential to the credibility of the commission that its programs be directed toward reforms, the need for which is felt by the government and reflected in Parliament.
The commission will be independent in its methods of working, in the establishment of its programs and in the conclusions which it reaches. The bill does not permit the Minister of Justice to control how the commission will perform its work once its programs and priorities are set. It does not permit the Minister of Justice to determine how its research shall be conducted. It does not permit the government or the Minister of Justice in any way to determine the recommendations which will be forthcoming from the commission.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The bill contemplates that the commission will consult broadly with the judiciary, members of the bar and persons engaged in teaching, research in legal and allied fields and with other interested bodies, including members of the public at large. The bill provides for the tabling of the commission's reports to the minister. It provides for the tabling of the annual report to the minister; and it provides for the tabling in Parliament of the program and studies approved by the minister.
In other words, the activities of the commission become the property of the people of Canada, through Parliament, in three stages. Once the program of studies is agreed upon by the commission, with the approval of the Minister of Justice, that program of studies must be tabled by the minister in Parliament and become public knowledge, and will be available to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and to Parliament as a whole.
Secondly, the commission must render an annual report to the Minister of Justice. The minister is bound to table that report on the floor of this House; and again that report will be made available to Parliament, presumably through the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and on the floor of the House.
Finally-and this is most important-any report on any particular study made to the minister must be tabled by the minister, again in the House of Commons, where it will become available to Parliament and its committees.

Mr. Speaker, the objects of the Commission are specified in the bill. Indeed, its mandate will be to study and keep under review on a continuing and systematic basis the statutes and other laws and to make recommendations for their improvement, modernization and reform.
February 23, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill
Without however, restricting the general scope of the above-mentioned objects, it may suggest especially the removal of anachronisms and anomalies in the law.
The Commission may also concern itself with the reflection in the law of the distinctive concepts and institutions of common law and civil law, as well as with the reconciliation, in the expression and application of the law, of the differences and discrepancies arising out of the differences between those two concepts or those two institutions.
I believe it to be a most important matter, since the federal judicial system should reflect both legal systems. It is therefore essential that the federal laws of the future not only be translations, but the reflection of both cultures and both concepts of law.
At the present time, when a bill or a policy to be put into a bill comes before the Department of Justice, the task is entrusted to a French-speaking editor familiar with the Civil Code, and an English-speaking editor, a lawyer versed in common law. The two versions are prepared at the same time and compared not specially for translation of words but for correspondence of concepts in both legal systems.
Thanks to that new commission for the reform of the laws, our federal legislative system will be not only bilingual but also bijural, that is will incorporate both legal systems.
Besides, the commission will be responsible for eliminating obsolete laws.
Finally, it will see to the development of new approaches to and new concepts of the law in keeping with and responsive to the changing needs of modern Canadian society and of individual members of that society.

It is contemplated that the commission may undertake joint projects with all other law reform commissions both abroad and at the provincial level. Several people with whom I talked before we drafted this legislation stressed the importance of not limiting the work of the commission strictly to the federal statutes but that we should keep in mind the general purview of the administration of justice that might involve the joint responsibility of the provinces.
There are a number of areas of the law that come quickly to mind. I could conceive of the necessity of having joint provincial legislation to back up the civil remedies enforcing the right to privacy. I could conceive a joint
[Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton).l
provincial legislation that would be necessary to reconcile our systems of evidence-criminal evidence, which is the responsibility of the federal government, and civil evidence, which redounds to the provinces.
The commission will be competent, in cooperation with provincial law reform commissions, to review these joint areas of the law. I hope that in this way the commission may be able to provide some measure of co-ordination in the general area of law reform in Canada. Such co-ordination appears to be desirable since there is still in Canada a relatively small pool of qualified persons in the form of legal experts upon which to draw.
As a matter of fact, the deans of Canadian law schools and the Association of Canadian Law Professors are somewhat concerned that the impetus toward law reform may well put tremendous pressures on the pool of legal resources and research in this country. I hope that the eventual chairman of this commission will, at an early opportunity, discuss with the Association of Canadian Law Professors and with the deans means to ensure that in planning a program of legal research and a program of reform they proceed in such way as not to place an immediate burden on law schools in Canada, to the detriment of law students. I think it is important that the primary responsibility of the academic profession in law remains the students in law, and that the necessary taking of their talents for the purpose of public law reform be done in such way as not to interfere with the curricula and programs of the law schools of this country. It is my hope that this law reform commission in Canada will mean that the law will never again stand still in this country; that we will have a body of experts able to suggest reforms in the law on a continuing rather than on an episodic basis.
What I mean is this. There are certain branches of the law that are so complicated in their federal aspects that it is virtually impossible at the departmental level to give them the necessary complete review from section one to section 1,000, or from A to Z. Immediately, I think of the Criminal Code of Canada, which is in need of thorough housekeeping, thorough revision, not merely in lawyers' law as it applies to the Criminal Code but also in many of the Code's social aspects.
Although the Department of Justice will continue to try to meet policy problems as they arise and to anticipate those policy problems, as we are going to do in a month or so
February 23, 1970	COMMONS
in a new criminal law reform bill which relates to bail, to the right to privacy and so on, I think it is necessary that in the medium and in the long term there be a permanent body that is able to review statutes such as the Criminal Code, and to bring forward a consistent piece of legislation.
We have set up a new research section in the Department of Justice. This research section will have as its duty to research the law, to anticipate and to fulfil policy initiatives which we in the Department of Justice will have to take. I hope to be able to announce shortly the name of a director of this new research section. I also hope to be able to announce a new reorganization of the Department of Justice which will reflect the establishment of this research section.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I have always felt that in looking at the Department of Justice, the Attorney General's side has been stronger than that of the Minister of Justice. That is to say, that part of the department which acts as lawyer to the government and to the various departments of government, and prosecutes on behalf of the people of Canada in the enforcement of federal statutes, has been a stronger branch of the Department of Justice than has been that of the reform and research side of the law. We hope we will be able in this new research section to promote that aspect of reform and thereby provide liaison between the Department of Justice on a daily, short-term policy basis with an overview, if I might use the words of the President of the Privy Council earlier this afternoon, of the federal statutes as represented by the Law Reform Commission.
So, the establishment of this law reform commission in no way will derogate from the responsibility of the federal Department of Justice to anticipate and meet the policy of law reform within federal jurisdiction. I want to suggest that I hope the bill reflects the government's genuine concern about the serious and continuing improvement and reform of Canadian federal law.
I suggest as immediate priorities that the commission should have a complete rewriting of the Criminal Law as one of its' first projects. I mention also the necessity of revising, on a total basis, the Canada Evidence Act and, in doing so, arrange that the criminal laws on evidence correspond in so far as that is possible with the civil law on evidence across Canada, both within the civil law

I should think it is incumbent upon the commission at an early stage to examine public administrative laws in Canada, the workings of federal boards, commissions and tribunals, as well as the remedies of the citizen by way of administrative review and judicial review. I think this House, in a report of the committee chaired by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) studying statutory instruments, has shown how Parliament might better review some of its administrative procedures. I think we have to buttress this on a local and national basis.
I hope I have been able, in a general way, to outline to the House the purposes and general contours of the bill. If the House decides in its wisdom to move this bill forward into committee, then of course members from all sides of the House, who contributed to what I might term the outstanding work under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie) of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, will be able to examine this bill in the detail which I hope it deserves.
Mr. R. Gordon L. Fairwealher {Fundy-Roy-al): Mr. Speaker, perhaps we should have a Member of Parliament on the law reform committee to shake the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) out of his boots. However, I will not destroy an obviously cooperative mood with that suggestion.
I think the House will appreciate, particularly those who have sat here for some time, the difficulty that so often is encountered by governments and by parliamentarians in translating ideas for reform into amendments to statutes or new statutes. The idea of continuing reform is an excellent one. It is one I may say that already operates not only in the state of New York but in the province of Ontario through its commission.
I also think of the Ontario government, and I am not making a big pitch here because it had its lumps during the weekend from a certain conference, was helped by the very special work done by former Chief Justice McRuer. His report will be of great value not only to this commission's work but to the administration of justice throughout Canada.
When one thinks of continuing reform of the law, one of course thinks of the tremendous work done in the private sector-nongovernment sector would be a better expression-by the American law institute and, I am
February 23, 1970

Law Reform, Commission Bill afraid to a lesser degree, by the commissioners on uniformity in our own country. I found, when I had office and hoped to get the commissioners to act, that speed in their case was very deliberate indeed. In other words, provincial governments would be interested in moving ahead on a particular issue in concert with other provinces but it would take the commissioners so long to translate the ideas into statute form, and then the ten legislatures to get around to doing anything about it, that we tended to circumvent the work on uniformity, and go about it on an individual basis.
I was very interested, and I think this is an assessment we should keep in mind, in the minister's idea of not making a career out of positions on this commission. I have been discussing with friends the fact that in 1969 not one of the graduates of the Harvard Law School went to what is known as the great law firms of the city of New York. Anybody who is interested in law schools and their graduates knows that usually the large, busy and prosperous law firms literally line up in Cambridge or elsewhere seeking the best brains from that and other important schools. This year, and I think this is very significant and shows an interesting new development of students, graduates prefer to work where the action is, so to speak. They prefer to work for Ralph Nader on the reforms that he is bringing about in respect to auto safety and protection of consumers' rights, and with organizations such as NAACP and others in the civil rights field for the black people of the United States. I hope very much that this type of orientation will pervade Canada's law schools. I think there is a great deal of evidence that it is beginning to occur here. In other words, this profession that some of us belong to is not primarily one for earning money. It is a profession which lends itself to a great deal of useful community activity. I think it is right that the minister does not sort of entrench his "tigers", because tigers too can get lazy if they lie in the sun too long. I should think that the commission should be transfused very often with new blood.
The other aspect, and I am sure the minister will keep this in mind, is the need for the use of what I might call the cross discipline aspect of law reform. For too long I think, lawyers have thought of the law as their preserve. This is by no means the case. I hope very much that when the minister gets around to amending the criminal law, for instance, a great deal of attention will be paid

to the useful and perceptive suggestions of others in the community engaged with crime and its results.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Many of us had the privilege the other evening, for example, of hearing a talk by a very remarkable young lady Miss Barbara Buck, who is devoting an important part of her life to work with drug addicts at Digger House in Toronto. Her discipline is not of the law; she is a sociologist. I was very impressed, however, by the very practical and knowledgeable way in which this young lady addressed herself to this serious social problem.
Although this will require joint provincial action, I would hope, in what the minister categorized as sort of a joint program, the minister would take into consideration the administration of justice in so far as the courts and all aspects of trial are concerned. In my own province, the judicature act was largely designed around the horse and buggy concept in the real sense of that term. The courts opened on Tuesday because in order to get to the centre where the court was located one had to start on Sunday. No one would think of travelling on Sunday so the court started on Tuesday. That is only a small aspect of a total problem.
I think many of us were shocked, for instance, by a situation which may be manifested in other parts of the country, although it occurred in Toronto. An accused person waited I believe some five or six months in the Don jail before being brought to trial. Obviously, in any reform in respect of this type of situation the commission would have to have very close contact with the provinces because of the constitution.
As to reporting certain segments of law reform undertaken by the commission, the minister I believe has undertaken that these reports will come to Parliament. This is an important departure. This is possibly just another cliche, but I would say this change is just the tip of the iceberg. The more governments find it necessary to have their work done by consultants, the more important it is that the results of this research get out to the public in some way. This is another subject for another time, but I think the minister is entitled to be congratulated for seeing, so far as this commission is concerned, that there will be no sitting on reports. As we reform the law I believe it it very important that the rationalization for the reform have very wide
February 23, 1970	COMMONS
public discussion and by the representatives of the public who happen to sit in this Parliament.
I hope other departments will follow this very useful precedent. There really should be no secret documents in a democratic state unless those documents literally have to do with the security of the state. I have never understood the passion for secrecy in our system in Canada and in the United Kingdom. If the commission on law reform can break through this type of secrecy, we will have accomplished a great deal.
This is about all I have to say. I am struck by the problems being faced in the United States today concerning the whole matter of the administration of justice and how really delicate and tenuous are some of the rights which are grandly proclaimed in rigid constitutions. This perhaps is wide-ranging, but I believe people who seek to list our liberties on a piece of paper should remember that it really did not matter very much, for example, if one was a United States citizen of Japanese origin or a Canadian of Japanese origin in World War II. Although one group was protected by the constitution of the United States and the other was protected by our jurisprudence each were extremely shabbily dealt with by the state.
So when I see people who want to have pieces of paper to put on the walls listing their rights-I am not condemning anyone who sees it in that way-I believe we must remember that rights can have a way of being twisted by governments which only pay lip service to them. I do not suppose Mr. Speaker would allow any more philosophizing, for instance about the results of the recent trials in Chicago and New York, but as we reform the law we should remember that it is the ethic of the country that supports the reform of law and this ethic will be very important in the days ahead.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic Party welcome Bill C-186 to establish a law reform commission, but we do so with reservations because we do not want to see the law reform commission become a stalling device for immediate and necessary legislation. In his remarks, the minister stated that he is fulfilling a commitment made in 1968 to the students of Osgoode Hall that he would bring in this bill within 18 months. He has now done so. I recall when I came down to Ottawa for the first time in 1965, the ten minister of justice promised complete revision of the Criminal Code. To

Law Reform Commission Bill
date we have had the omnibus bill which certainly brought forth measures which were welcome and necessary in respect of the criminal law. Today, we have a statement by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) to the effect that he hopes to bring forth another bill in the near future concerning bail and arrest. In the interim, we have had the Ouimet commission which studied criminal law in Canada and which presented an excellent report concerning changes which it believes should take place.
I hope the present minister will not await a report by the law reform commission before implementing some of the recommendations contained in the Ouimet commission report. I can think at this moment very quickly of the right to counsel at trial. This is a very important aspect of the criminal law which has been neglected in Canada. When the minister brings forth the second bill on law reform, I hope it will include not only the matter of bail and arrest but also the right to counsel at trial.
There are three ways to reform the law. First, a special committee or commission could be set up to examine a particular matter, or a standing committee such as the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs could be set up or a permanent commission could be appointed. This bill would appoint a permanent commission. In respect of the first method, that of setting up a special committee of the House of Commons to examine a particular matter, I think immediately of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons that was set up to study the divorce laws in Canada.
As a result of the recommendations of this joint committee the divorce law in Canada has been brought up to the point of the law of divorce in England as set forth in the year 1870. Even at this stage, after the divorce laws have been changed, many hardships and grievances remain for some members of the community. It was only as a result of the work of this committee that the divorce laws were changed. I can think of the Ouimet Commission which studied the criminal law and recommended changes. I can think of the commission which was set up at least six years ago to study juvenile delinquency and which submitted a report in 1966. However, from that time until the present there have been no amendments to the Juvenile Delinquents Act. I can only approve this bill with reservation when I think of the urgency to amend the juvenile delinquents legislation in

[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The establishment of a standing committee is necessary to study the reform of the law. We have done this through the establishment of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. That standing committee has many shortcomings, one of which is the lack of research facilities, but I can recall that there has been a study in depth of certain subjects that affect many Canadians. We had a study with regard to bail; another one with regard to drugs, and a third one on expunging criminal records. The committee submitted reports in those three areas as a result of the studies.
The minister said with regard to bail that measures will be brought forth. I cannot be too critical of that. We are now awaiting a report from another committee that was set up by the government to study the use of drugs. With regard to expunging criminal records, a bill was presented by the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) which, however, is not in keeping with the thinking of the members of the committee on justice and legal affairs. In fact, the principle of the bill is totally contrary to their recommendations.
We have now before us Bill C-186 which sets forth the necessary framework for a permanent commission. As I said, we in the NDP welcome it provided it is not a stalling device, because there is no reason for a further delay in setting up a permanent law reform commission. We live now in a society where rapid technological, economic and social changes are taking place, a situation which has created a continuous shift in our way of life. Our legal system has failed to keep abreast of these sweeping changes. Many of our laws are couple; many are uncertain and often many are not adapted to our changing world. We operate under the law of precedents. It might be of interest to members of the House to know that in England there are one quarter of a million recorded cases that are used as precedents, and in addition we have statutes, regulations, orders in council and bylaws on three levels of government. Is it any wonder then that our law is not in keeping with the changing times?
I should like to refer to an article written by Allen M. Linden called "The Laggard Law: Machinery of Law Reform". He summed up by saying:
The present machinery of law reform in Canada is rusty and obsolescent; horse and buggy methods

are being used in a jet age. Efforts to keep the law responsive to societal aspirations are lagging because of limited resources, non-existent vehicles for reform, overworked public officials, and self-satisfaction.
The same author warns us as follows: Unless new institutions are established to transform our law to embody the aspirations of the majority of the Canadian people, our legal system will be in danger. Therefore, the time has come to create the machinery to expedite the intelligent growth and steady modification of law and legal procedure.
Here we are in 1970 passing a bill to set up a law reform commission. The minister mentioned consultations with officials from the state of New York. It is interesting to note that tire state of New York passed such legislation in 1934; that New Zealand passed it in 1937; California in 1953; and the great province of Ontario in 1964. As the minister stated, a law reform Commission bill was passed in England in 1965 and was enacted on the 750th anniversary of Magna Carta. With regard to the federal government, a bill was presented in 1965 by Richard A. Bell, a former Conservative member, but the bill did not go beyond first reading. In 1966, the Canadian Bar Association recommended the setting up of a law reform commission. The Ontario law reform commission has done an excellent job in the studies that it has undertaken, and has prepared about four or five reports. It prepared a report on the mechanics lien act, the perpetuities act, the personal property security act and the expropriation act. I think that their bill and their report on expropriation helped in no small measure in passing the federal Expropriation Act, which is similar in many areas.
The bill before us proposes, as the minister pointed out, the appointment of four full time members to the commission and two part time members. With regard to their qualifications there is a requirement that the chairman and vice-chairman, one to be full time and one part time, be judges or barristers with ten years' experience. This is one aspect which I would like the minister to take under advisement because the initiative with regard to the reform of the law has come from younger members of the bar and in many cases from academics in law schools across Canada, academics who have the time and the research facilities necessary to study the laws in depth.
On looking at the particular clause in the bill setting down the necessary qualifications of the chairman and vice-chairman we see that they must be a judge or a barrister. I

think the minister would be well advised to take into account law professors and law teachers for those positions. We have a precedent in the Ontario law reform commission. Mr. Allan Leal, Q.C., is the chairman and has been a practising barrister for some years. He then became dean of Osgoode law school and is now chairman of the Ontario law reform commission. It would be fair to say that he is doing an excellent job as its chairman. He is an academic with past practical experience. On that committee in Ontario, not only do we have an academic in Mr. Leal but we have a former chief justice of the high court, the Hon. James C. McRuer. At the present time the other members of the Ontario committee are the Hon. Richard A. Bell, W. Gibson Gray and William R. Pool. I would ask the minister to take into account what I think is a shortcoming, namely, the absence of any law professor or other academic.

The objects of the commission are set forth on page 5 of the bill. The first of these is the "removal of anachronisms in the law." I think it was Dickens who said that the law is an ass. Many people think that sometimes the practitioners of the law can also be included in that class. It is because of the anachronisms in the law that we, as legislators, have taken the initiative to remove them, and to remove obsolete laws from the statute books. Another stated object is "reflection in the law". Lord knows, we certainly need reflection in depth in the law. Another object is "the development of new approaches." One area in which we have to develop a new approach is that of the uniformity of laws across Canada. One would hope to see a codification of the law of contract, the law of torts, and the law dealing with land titles. When I heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) condemn lawyers with reference to land law as practised in Ontario, especially with reference to the registration of legal instruments, it made me realize there is a dire necessity to up date the law of land and the procedure for registration of legal instruments in Ontario.
It is necessary to have uniformity with regard to securities legislation. At the moment we have ten different provinces enacting legislation with regard to securities.
Law Reform Commission Bill I would hope that the Law Reform Commission would direct its attention to basic security legislation which would prevail across the whole of Canada.
The provinces have passed laws with regard to compensation for the victims of criminal violence. We have a hodge-podge of different statutes covering compensation for victims of criminal violence. I recall that the minister said he would take up this subject with the provincial attorneys general during the summer, and try to get some uniformity in that area. I would hope we could have that uniformity so that when people are injured as the result of criminal violence in any province they will get just and equitable treatment.
I think it would be fair to say that the Law Reform Commission should give priority to laws which have an impact on individuals. It should give a priority not only to the area of criminal law but to many other areas which concern the freedoms we enjoy in Canada. I personally would like to see the commission take another look at the philosophy underlying criminal law. In the past we have had the adversary approach, and many people believe this falls far short in providing any basis upon which the reformation and rehabilitation of offenders may be considered. We have taken a half step with regard to juvenile delinquents. Now we look more at the reformation and rehabilitation aspect rather than merely at the commission of an offence by a juvenile delinquent. After reading a few books by psychiatrists and others indicating the shortcomings of the adversary approach, I would hope the commission would study this matter in depth so that we can meet some of the problems that are facing Canadians.
With respect to the current interest in the expungement of criminal records, I believe this interest would not have developed but for the fact that more first offenders are to be found in all classes in the community. For years young men in the lower income groups who had convictions registered against them had to face all the restrictions that were imposed on them with regard to employment, travel and bonding. In the past few years, however, a wider segment of the community has been involved in criminal offences. We have had the white collar frauds, and the impaired driving convictions to consider. These types of convictions affect another class, and now a first attempt is being made in the area of expunging criminal records.
February 23, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill
The minister said that the commission will present an annual report, which will be tabled in the House, and that it will also present reports of particular studies it makes. We welcome this. 1 would ask him to look at the British precedent in this regard, and more especially with regard to reports that are tabled on particular studies. In the British house, not only is a report tabled but sometimes it is accompanied with the comments of the Minister of Justice. Sometimes it is not only necessary to have a commission study a particular question but it is also necessary to have the Minister of Justice review that study and make comments on it. Otherwise, the government may be saddled with the commission's report, presented to the minister and tabled in the House. Under this legislation the minister should be given power to add any recommendations or comments that he may wish to make. This is the English practice, and I think it is a good one. The legislative supremacy of Parliament should never be undermined by the reports of commissions. I am sure there will be adequate protection in this legislation in that respect. When reports are tabled in the House I hope they will be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, so that further representations from organized bodies and other interested people may be heard.
Another thing we must remember is that mere setting up of a Law Reform Commission does not mean we should do away with or undermine other commissions and committees that have been established. I am sure the minister knows this and will keep it in mind. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the law reform commission legislation we are now studying will justify the hopes and the expectations of the minister, of the members of this House, and of the Canadian public.
.[Translation]

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS AND DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very pleased with the introduction of this bill today, because we have been waiting for it for a long time. I congratulate the minister for having fulfilled one of the promises he made to us in 1968. I was a member of Parliament then and I remember. I think that it is the first time that a minister is true to his promise; many promises of this type have been made to us in the past.
In 1965-66, the same promise had been made to us and we were still waiting for the establishment of this Commission. We are happy to learn that this will be a permanent organization; today, the rhythm of life is so

quick and change is so rapid that it is absolutely essential that a Commission of this type be permanently established in order to attempt to up-date our laws.
Mr. Speaker, this Commission will likely operate much the same way as other commissions do. It will make inquiries across the country to sound public opinion. I hope that the witnesses who will come before the comi-missioners will be listened to carefully and that their testimony will serve some useful purpose towards the proposed reform. I cannot imagine that a commission is created merely for the pleasure of conducting studies or travelling across Canada. First of all, it is essential to know what people think about justice. It is certain that several persons administer it, but one must not forget above all else that the people suffer the consequences of its application. Therefore, it is at the people's level that we must seek basic ideas in order to adapt justice to the people's living conditions.
It interested me greatly to hear the minister say that the Commission would try to make a synthesis of our two legal systems in order to find a common denominator. I was happy to hear him say those things because he is definitely one of those who perceive disparities existing within Canada itself.
Too often today do we hear government authorities repeat that Quebec is a province like all the others and that Canada is an unusual country. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) just proved that in Canada there are really two cultures and two judicial systems and that we must not try to eliminate one in favour of the other but attempt to establish links between the two.
In my opinion, the Minister of Justice should be congratulated since he understood the nature of the problem and did not try to elude it. He studies the facts and attempts to make a synthesis of them. This is a real good start on the standpoint of justice if an effort is made to understand better the various mentalities in Canada which is such a large country to administer, as all the English provinces, as everybody knows, are under the common law while the Civil Code applies to the province of Quebec.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I think he made a very interesting point there and I wish him, and the commission particularly, much success as the task is a difficult one and it will be hard work achieving a synthesis that reflects the true situation of law in Canada.
February 23, 1970

We laymen wonder how long it will be before the commission comes up with results. If I could ask a favour of the commission, it would be that it tackle the job as early as possible. In fact, the creation of such a commission, to guide the Department of Justice and also to help bring about a new code of laws was long overdue. I feel the commission should act without delay and take all possible steps to speed up its work and submit its report.
It is said that the commission will report every year. I think that if the official report is to be handed in every year, the commission must keep in constant touch with the department and that, as soon as the study of a subject is over and done with, it must report to the Department of Justice that will take it up to the House and will attempt to apply its recommendations.
A complete review of our judicial system was necessary. If we just leaf through the Code, we will be shocked by the number of sections that are obsolete. I think it a must to review it thoroughly and I hope such review will be conducted with order and clarity.
The new code should use clear vocabulary. In certain fields, particularly that of justice, it would seem that people who draft legislation do their utmost to find complicated expressions and to use incomprehensible language.
In my opinion, it would be possible to write legislation in a general way and still make the text simple enough so that everyone will understand; this would do away with arguments about terminology whose only result is to enable lawyers to prolong cases and quarrel among themselves, as I have seen them do myself. Indeed, I always found it tiresome to see them arguing for days to try to establish the exact meaning of a word.
It seems to me that the English and French languages are rich enough so that an end can be put to the obscureness of legal texts.
Certain priorites will have to be determined in that study. We have done so in the past. Some ministers of justice have advocated certain reforms here in the House. They claimed they were priorities. But we did not consider them priorities but merely promises. When the Criminal Code was amended, especially with regard to abortion and homosexuality, I did not consider them priorities, although some seemed to think that they should come first. Still, it was done, and I am sure that the members of the commission who will be appointed will be able to determine the priorities and then do the work that is required.

Law Reform Commission Bill
As I said a while ago, there has been concern about old matters, specially with regard to expressions that are still popular such as "air pirates". It is shocking to think that the civil code cannot include measures on that because it falls under the Criminal Code. The commission will have to deal with such matters to bring our laws up to date.
I hope the new code will be less punitive and more remedial, and that the social character of the law will be stressed. One must realize that the steel age and the muscle age are a thing of the past. We now live in the atomic age, the age of intelligence. And I feel that our laws must reflect this. The criminal must no longer be treated like a criminal. In former times, it was said of criminals that they were not like other men. The new code must treat them like mentally ill people and especially like human beings, taking into consideration their essence, their intelligence. Then we will have taken a wonderful step towards renewing and humanizing the Criminal Code, to my mind the greatest stride ever towards law reform.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS AND DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that every member of this House will enthusiastically support this important proposal for legal reform which has been made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) in the introduction of this bill. The minister has referred to some of the issues which might be studied by the proposed law reform commission such as the Criminal Code, the law of evidence and other matters. Each member who has spoken has added other issues which he regards as major and which call for study.
Following this pattern, I have one or two suggestions about major issues. They are based upon my experience, which has been rather extensive, in the study and application of federal statutes as a result of practising law in Ottawa for almost 20 years. One of the most appalling things about the present statutes of Canada is the lack of consistency and the lack of uniformity which characterizes many of the statutes. For example, in one statute a person who may be charged with a particular offence has the onus of proof cast upon him to show that he is innocent. In another statute where there may be an offence almost parallel in its terms, the onus is upon the Crown.
February 23, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill
There are hundreds of examples in our statutes where an important discretion is conferred upon a minister or a public official to make a decision. There are many different ways in which this discretionary power is conferred. What you might think would be the rule which would apply to the exercise of a discretion under one statute as a result of your experience, sometimes proves not to be the case because of some odd difference in the wording.
The operation and application of our statutes as a whole in relation to the rights and privileges of private citizens is something which should give great concern to all of us. This is now even more important because of the fact the Supreme Court of Canada, in an important recent decision, has given new life and vitality to the Canadian Bill of Rights.
As a major project of any law reform commission there should be a careful study of the statutes with a view to determining how they apply against individual citizens; how the rights of citizens are protected and enhanced in their dealings with their government; how the Bill of Rights applies to the statutes of Canada; and to what extent the statutes explicitly or implicitly recognize the Bill of Rights which in its most important sections is supposed to overrule statutory provisions which are in conflict with the fundamental rights of the people.
There are many big and popular issues which will engage the attention of this commission. I would not be surprised, following the practice of the Ontario Law Reform Commission, if the new federal commission became engaged in long and complex inquiries dealing with important and complex issues. As we know, the Ontario Commission had already published four large volumes and more are to follow. The very complexity of the inquiries that it has carried out, the difficulties of the subject matter and the difficulty of finding time, undoubtedly, in a parliamentary timetable to deal with its findings have of course slowed down the implementation of its recommendations. There is no way out of this problem because we all know that changes of a major nature in the law must be made only after careful study. If they are made precipitately and without due deliberation, they will not be satisfactory.
I hope this new commission will not concern itself only with big matters. I hope it will not be over-impressed by the fact it has the capacity to solve some of the larger legal problems of this country. I hope it will direct

its attention continuously and in detail to all the minor law reforms which it is necessary to make.
Our government operates according to law. It is governed in every respect by the statutes of Canada. Experience shows that in many instances, for one reason or another, the laws have become out of date. There may be some unexpected defect or imprecision in the drafting of a statute; some circumstances may not have been foreseen or some new circumstances may have arisen. I can recall many times in my practice in this city where, having presented a point of view to governmental officials, I was told and I had to agree that they had no alternative but to say, "Too bad we can't do what you want. We think we should be able to do it, but unfortunately the law does not give us this authority." In most of these circumstances, the number of people affected by this type of decision is small. It may be only one person or a very small number of persons who somehow or other have come within the purview of an obscure section of an act of Parliament.
I need not tell the members of this House that the correction of this kind of injustice and legal result is something which rarely happens in the experience of this Parliament. There are simply too many big and time-consuming issues which engage our attention for departments to continually, year after year, bring forward to this House small projects for the amendment of defects in the various statutes for which they are responsible.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I therefore feel that if the new commission directed its attention not only to big issues but to small ones it could confer great benefit upon the public of Canada as well as upon members of this House. Hon. members having read the bill will realize that the commission can act on its own account-that it can receive complaints from the public and take action. It will be in a position to make reports from time to time which will inform members of this House and of the public of problems which have arisen in the administration of sections of particular statutes. This kind of legislative reform could, perhaps, be wrapped up in a single bill, a miscellaneous law amendment statute-something which would not involve the House in a discussion of great principle. In passing it, we would be doing necessary housekeeping so as to keep the law up to date. In this way, the commission could exercise a great function in ensuring that justice is done not only to the mass of the people
February 23. 1970

but to individuals. It might become, indeed, a legislative ombudsman whose work would be of great assistance to us all.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS AND DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, anyone on this continent who in the course of the last few weeks, and in particularly in the last ten days or so, has had occasion to observe the proceedings in Chicago, must have come to the conclusion that it was high time we in this country, as well as those in the United States, took a completely new look at where we stand on this issue of the status of the courts, and law and order.
In Chicago were represented the two extremes of a certain position. Between those two extremes the average person stands appalled, shocked and amazed at the spectacle presented of a courtroom in which the defendants and their counsel brought the programs of violence and confrontation which have been witnessed outside; where one of the defendants had to be literally bound and gagged, if I remember correctly, and where at the conclusion of the proceedings counsel for the defendants were sent to jail, one of them for a term of four years.
I have tried to read objectively the newspaper accounts of this affair, and I have listened to the radio and television accounts of what took place. It seems to me that the law and order faction was represented by a very repressive element. Obviously, if there is to be respect for the judicial system in the western world, and particularly on this continent, and respect for the statutes passed by freely-elected representatives of the people, there has to be change. If this sort of thing is re-enacted, and it appears there is every likelihood that it will be re-enacted all over the country, it will lead to a breakdown of the judicial process. More important than anything else, it will mean a loss of the respect people have for the judicial system.
My experience in the practice of law began when I was articled as a student at the age of 16. At that time, in the Province of Saskatchewan, there was a liquor enforcement act on the statute books, a silly, stupid law which did not reflect the thinking and the mores of the people. This was the law which replaced the prohibition legislation which had existed earlier.
What happened was this: all the respectable people were breaking this law over and over again. 1 remember those early days of complete prohibition. The way to buy a bottle of liquor then was to go to the local drug store. For $2 a physician would sign a large number

Law Reform Commission Bill of forms-prescriptions-and these would enable anyone to buy liquor as medicine. This is not the kind of system which leads to respect for the functioning of the judicial process or for statutes passed by a legislature. People lost all respect for the law and for those who administered it; it was a question of seeing whether one could beat the system. Bearing in mind what has taken place in Chicago, we need not feel sympathy for the extremists on either side. But we must feel sympathy for the people in the middle who are entitled to look to the judicial process and to reasonable and proper enforcement of good laws which are passed for their protection, health and assistance.
I have no hesitation in telling the minister that I approve of this bill in principle. I think it is capable of doing a great deal of good. But the commission will, I feel, be faced with some extraordinary problems for which it will need to find solutions in short order. For this reason I hope it will not be too remote- that it will not look at the situation from an ivory tower. This has been one of our problems in relation to laws which are passed from time to time-I have in mind amendments in statutes designed to block loopholes, to cross t's, to provide for situations not contemplated when legislation was originally passed. All too often we do not take into account the real impact of such actions upon the people most affected. It is fine to have people with judicial or legal knowledge appointed to this commission but I think it would be even better, perhaps, if we were to appoint for instance, a convict who had been rehabilitated, or a bankrupt who had made financial restitution.
What I am trying to say is that membership of the commission should include people who have some personal understanding of what these laws mean to those who are likely to be directly affected by them. In any event, the commission should make sure that they or their representatives get into the streets and talk to the people. I think it was Jeremy Bentham who said laws should be enacted so that they brought the greatest good to the greatest number. There are so many things which the commission might consider. There is the question of insanity-the application of the M'Naghten rule today; the increasing use of alcohol, the increasing use of drugs. What will be the impact of these changes both on the criminal law and on the civil law to the extent that it comes under federal supervision?
February 23, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I recall the case a number of years ago of a man who was successful in having a charge of murder reduced to manslaughter because the court found his degree of intoxication when he committed the crime was such that he was incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of his act. This is not a defence which would have permitted him to be acquitted, but it did permit what would otherwise have been a charge of murder to be reduced to a charge of manslaughter. We will also have to look at the extent to which people commit acts under the influence of drugs. The formidable increase in the use of drugs of one kind or another is bound to leave its impact on the actions and conduct of those who use them.
I hope that in an issue of this kind the minister will either recommend to the commission or that the commission will consider, as I think they quite properly should, the contracting out of further inquiries to be undertaken by private individuals or groups. I think an immediate study should be commissioned by the commission into the whole question of legal competence and responsibility involving cases of insanity, use of drugs and so on.
I have noticed that one or two courts have used television to publicize their proceedings. I am not proposing the general use of television in our courts, but I think that on a trial basis it might be useful to bring home to the people the actual processing of legal disputes, whether in our criminal courts or otherwise. The courts are growing increasingly unfamiliar to the people.
It has been my fortunate experience to be involved in the study and practice of law in a great many small communities, communities where you knew the people and those who administered the courts; communities where juries were usually personally known to most of those who were unfortunate enough to be caught up in the criminal law. I think this condition had its usefulness, though it is not so prevalent today. All too often people today have the idea that law is remote, is austere, and sometimes far too antiseptic. I think the two safeguards which are available to the ordinary people are the legislative and parliamentary process-which I may suggest, as an aside, is slowly being scuttled; but more of that later-and the judicial process. Certainly the judicial process is tremendously important.
The statutes that are being set up through the legislative process must come increasingly under the scrutiny of a commission of this kind. However, I suggest to the minister that it might be very useful to have some liaison in this regard. I know that the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) facetiously suggested placing a member of the House of Commons on the commission-I think he was being facetious in that regard. However, it seems to me that there is some scope for liaison here.
The present Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs has in many instances acted quite objectively and done a good job in may respects. It is my hope that this practice will continue and that, Parliament by Parliament, this committee will become one of the important committees of the House of Commons. This is the committee that will, in due course, be studying in detail the statutes that the government may see fit to bring down following recommendations by the commission. I think some thought might be given to having some form of informal liaison from time to time between the commission and the members of the standing committee. This would be very useful at a later date.
For example, let me deal with some of the suggestions that have been made. The world has known for some years of the dangers that are inherent in the voyaging of large tankers to different parts of the world. For 12 years we have had available to us under international conventions the right to lay down regulations governing the innocent passage of vessels, even the innocent passage of foreign vessels, into Canadian waters. It seems to me that by now it would have been possible to lay down rules, regulations and statutes consequent upon consideration of the subject by a committee of this kind. This would afford those thousands of people so deeply affected and greatly injured by what happened recently off the coast of Cape Breton Island means by which they would have recourse to some compensation. I venture to say that today, faced with the necessity of taking legal proceedings in the civil court against either the owners of the vessel of their insurers, many people would simply forget about it. The world has known about this particular problem for a long enough period now for some action to have been taken. There should have been available some means to enable private citizens to have some recourse to compensation without the dangers and anxieties that arise in litigation that

February 23, 1970

involves the expenditure of large sums of money.
I should like to suggest to the minister that while we do not want unduly to speed up contemplation by the commission of the sorts of things that are covered within the four corners of the commission's terms of reference, nevertheless once the commission has come to conclusions and made recommendations, the government should see that these recommendations are made public. It may well be that the commission itself would make them public; but I think that all too often the public have become disillusioned over the length of time involved, the gestation period as it were, between the time that someone gets an idea about dealing with a certain problem and the time it first sees the light of day in this House. Consequently, as I say, the public loses its confidence and trust.
In the course of his remarks, the minister dealt with the proposals that were made by the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments. It is true, as the minister said, that some of the recommendations of that committee outlined proposals with which this House should deal. There were 23 recommendations, 18 of which involved proposals with which the government should deal. Now, I know there are problems of personnel and manpower. Nevertheless, it is now over a year since this committee was set in motion. It was a good committee, non-partisan and objective, a committee that made a united and unanimous report.
I suggest that some of the proposals made in that report should have been implemented by now. If not, then at least the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), in his capacity as house leader, should have brought them before the House for discussion. This report followed years of research, of discussion, of requests made by members of the House who had felt for too long that, while we have ways and means through standing committees for dealing with laws, we really have no effective way of dealing with the substantial, in fact overwhelming, extent to which the lives of the people of this country are affected by regulations.
I think that the bill with which we are dealing does bear this point in mind. I notice that one clause makes reference to "statutes and other laws". I think those who framed the bill had in mind doing something about the extent to which the legislation dealt with orders in council, decrees and regulations.
Law Reform Commission Bill
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
What are some of the things that were recommended? It was recommended that regulations made in the exercise of the prerogative power of the governor in council be subject to the same procedures and requirements. This is something long overdue for discussion. It was recommended that there should be no exemptions from the requirements of the Regulations Act. I am sure that the Minister of Justice will do a good job, but it was recommended that he should be charged with the responsibility of deciding for all regulation making authorities which documents should be classified as regulations.
It was recommended that departmental directives and guidelines as to the exercise of discretion under a statute or regulation where the public is directly affected should be published. What is the use of having a law if you do not publish it to let people know what it is? We should not be like the Roman emperor who, when compelled to publish his laws, had them engraved upon a tablet which was then hoisted so high nobody could read it. That is our situation today in respect of regulations, and orders in council. I do not blame the minister for this situation because I think he is well disposed towards this particular problem. However, if the attitude of this government towards this committee's report is an indication of the way in which the government is going to treat recommendations of the law reform commission, then we are beaten before we start. In that case, we should forget the whole thing and scrap the bill. The indications at this stage of the session are that the government will probably not bring its proposals before Parliament until near the end of the session. Then, the session will end and we will have to start all over again. I think it is a disgrace that this committee's reports which bear right on the issue brought up by the minister should be allowed to wither on the vine in this way.
I give the minister full credit for desiring to deal with this issue in order that there might be more expeditious action in government terms once the commission has made recommendations. I understand the government is not necessarily bound by these recommendations. However, as in the case of the third report of the committee on statutory instruments, if the government does not like the recommendations, it should come out and say so. The government should indicate the view it takes and what parts of a report it does accept. It should then place the matter before
February 23, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill the House for debate and let the House decide on the issue. That is what this House is for, and that is what we were elected to do-consider, discuss, debate and then decide the issues. So, it should be with this law reform commission.
I wish the commission well and I urge upon the minister once more that the personnel of the commission, the people who are going to do the job of contemplating, ruminating and acting, should represent a cross-section of the community. I think it is tremendously important that the membership should include academics and professionals, as well as those who can be said to be truly representative of the great majority of people who will be affected. It is in that sense they will consider and recommend what ultimately will be translated into law, and it is in this sense that the great virtues of this proposal will be found. I hope the committee will consider these facts and make the changes which are needed. I urge the minister to concentrate on this idea when seeking the people who are to be members of this commission, because I think this is the true test of the success or failure of the proposals and objectives found in this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as it is late, I will only say a few words, leaving out the fine shades and distinctions which would be necessary.
To my mind, when the act to establish a commission for the reform of the laws of Canada is adopted, it will be a red letter day. The purpose of the Commission, as stated in clause 11(d) is as follows:
The development of new approaches to and new concepts of the Law in keeping with and responsive to the changing needs of modem Canadian society and of individual members of that society.
I feel that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) should be congratulated for having introduced such a bill.
But obviously, I did not wish to take the floor only to pay compliments; I also want to comment on the matter.
As far as I am concerned, the clause which outlines the objects of the Commission could be made more explicit. Also the bill should state in a more precise way the philosophy which underlies the development of the new methods mentioned in clause 11(d).
In fact, I believe that certain fundamental principles should be carefully spelled out in the Commission's mandate.


I also believe that this mandate should cover parliamentary procedure and the legislative process. In this way, we shall touch upon social and political sciences and I think that one disguises the truth when one says that the Department of Justice has never taken into account the progress of such sciences.
When clause 11(d) mentions the changing needs of modern society, it obviously refers to one of the main objects of social sciences, that is social change and the history of societies. In this regard, I believe the clause would be improved through a more precise wording.
If it is true that the philosophy that must be the basis of the Commission's activity should be more explicitly defined, I fail to understand why it is required that certain members of the Commission must have been members of the bar for at least ten years, when we know that youth today plays an important, even an essential role in the legal field and the scientific world.
I know some law faculties where most of the professors have been members of the bar for less than 10 years. In the United States Ralph Nader for instance, the barrister who has brought in the most drastic changes regarding the rights of consumers, has been a member of the bar for less than 10 years. I do not think that these two criteria are necessary.
Finally, I think that if democracy has a meaning, members of the Commission should be appointed at the discretion of the government, so that if the latter changes, the new Minister of Justice will be completely free to appoint other members since there should be a community of thought between political parties, at least regarding the main objectives.
I do not see why some members of the commission should be irremovable for a period of years.
Finally, to my mind, one of the reasons that make the passing of the bill necessary is, paradoxically, the lack of technical means provided for members of the House who are interested in the reform and updating of the laws. If members had had the means of doing this work, if they had them today, the commission would not have to be set up. I do not want to minimize the usefulness of the commission, but I think members could have achieved this task, had they been given the proper tools.
I would like the commission, the establishment of which is hoped for by all political
February 23, 1970	COMMONS
parties, to concern itself with both theoretical problems and the implementing of justice, in other words the democratization of justice.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to join only very briefly in the chorus of acceptance we have heard in respect of this bill. I believe it is long overdue. A law reform commission should have been in existence over the years. I do not say that as a condemnation of the minister because his term of office has not been very long. There are one or two things I should like to say about this particular bill. As has already been mentioned, the quality of those who serve on the commission will be of tremendous importance. I do not know whether this is the minister's view, but it is my view that the legal profession tends to be very conservative with a small "c". It does not tend to be reform-minded in any way. Certainly, that used to be the case. Whether or not it still is 1 am not sure. I see that the bill provides that a majority of the members should be persons who have been judges or lawyers with ten years' experience. I hope the minister will strive very hard to get younger people appointed to this commission, so that it will not be composed largely of senior people.
In the legal profession I think the tendency to be concerned about reform in any way is apparent among the younger generation and not among the senior generation of lawyers, by and large. It would seem to me that on this commission we need people with radical ideas. A law reform commission could very easily turn its attention to the tidying up here and there of little details. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Blair) seems to believe it is an important function. I do not think it is an important function. I believe such a commission should come up with radical ideas in respect of making the law more just in its application. I would hope that on the commission there would be members representing welfare and labour. They would represent the vast majority of the population. I believe the people who see the inside of a lawyer's office most often come from the top 10 per cent of our people. From my personal experience as a lawyer for many years I know that the average person tends to avoid going near a lawyer's office. This certainly has been true.
If we are to have thorough-going law reform, I think people who have had experi-21701-41
DEBATES	3975
Law Reform Commission Bill ence of the law at the labour and welfare level should be involved. I hope also that we will not forget about the academic people. For a long time in the legal profession there was sort of almost a contempt for those whose experience in law was largely academic. I would think the chairman of this commission should be a person who has had academic and judicial experience, perhaps someone like Mr. Justice Laskin if he should be available. In any event, the chairman should be a person of that type whose training has been in the theory and purpose of the law. For too long the legal profession has been complacent, concerning itself with what an excellent institution it is. The minister may have attended meetings of the Canadian Bar Association where the general tenor of the discussions seemed to be what a good service lawyers provide to the community. As a lawyer I would not belittle this attitude, but I do not think this sort of complacency is justified.
I hope the minister will seek out for the commission people who will be radical critics and not merely people who would become engaged in tidying up little pieces of legislation here and there. Another suggestion, which I believe was made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), is that one section of the commission should look almost exclusively into the question of the repeal of obsolete laws. I would like to see a rule in this House that we never bring in one law without repealing another, because we multiply laws without reason. I would like to see a thorough review made of the Statutes of Canada in an effort to find laws which are absolutely useless at the present time.
In conclusion, I should like to say that this law reform commission is an excellent idea. It is long overdue. It could give impetus to making this a more just society.
