subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO MAKE STRIKES ILLEGAL AND CREATE LABOUR TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to making strikes and lockouts illegal within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada and creating a special labour tribunal whose decision shall be final and binding on the parties for the term of an agreement to be arrived at or where there is no agreement, for the terms set by a Court appealed to for a judicial determination of the best and most just solution or arrangement for the parties.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I was prompted to submit this notice of motion because of some of the unhappy events of the last year or two, including the strike of the St. Lawrence Seaway workers, the grain handlers' strike at the head of the lakes, the grain handlers' strike at the west coast and innumerable other strikes which have had a very serious effect on markets, particularly export markets, for farm products.
At the outset I should like to quote from page 3 of the report of the task force on Canadian industrial relations:
1.	Periodically the conduct of labour-management relations in any country is subject to severe criticism. In Canada, as well as in many other western countries, the attack on collective bargaining has been mounting in recent years. The result verges on a crisis of confidence in the present Industrial relations system.
2.	Why has the public apparently lost faith in the prevailing collective bargaining process? The rash of strikes which have caught the headlines in

recent years provides much of the explanation. In many of these disputes the protagonists seem to suffer less than the public. Worse still, there is apprehension that the parties are using the public as their whipping boy while they work out theii differences.
3. Many of these stoppages have interrupted services seldom before affected by collective bargaining. Strikes by professionals-even doctors, nurses and teachers-have disturbed the public. So also have shutdowns in what have long been thought to be essential services, notably school, hospital and postal services.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
4.	Public misgiving has been aggravated further by violence that has accompanied some recent labour disputes. Pictures of trucks being overturned and of pickets and police scuffling has not helped the image of industrial relations.
5.	Nor can one minimize the damage done by corrupt and undemocratic practices which the Norris Commission revealed in the Seafarers, International Union of Canada. Added to earlier revelations of the unseemly conduct of certain unions in the United States, the publicity convinced many that organized labour was not the idealistic force for good that they had been led to believe.
6.	To these events must be added a public predisposition to blame unions and collective bargaining for inflation which has plagued the Canadian economy in recent years.
It seems ludicrous to me that in this country where we pay so much lip service to the cause of peace, law and order, we should continue to settle many of our most important disputes in our land by the use of raw power or force.
My proposal is that the government should give consideration to the outlawing of strikes and lockouts within the jurisdiction of federal Parliament and to the setting up of a special labour tribunal which would have power to help settle disputes and, if necessary, to make binding awards. Many of the critics of such proposals seem to assume that they are aimed solely at labour unions. This is most emphatically not the case, because in many instances employer groups are equally reluctant to accept these proposals. I prefer to argue that this proposition is aimed at neither labour nor management, but instead toward the welfare of all concerned and the country as a whole.
It is true that a settlement by binding arbitration would likely be unsatisfactory to one or both parties to the dispute, but it would only be binding for the term set out in the award and no doubt the matter would be reopened for negotiation after a breathing space or cooling off period approximating the term of the settlement. There would be an excellent possibility of renewed negotiations producing an amicable agreement. In the
February 23, 1970	COMMONS DEBATES
meantime, work and production would continue; no pay cheques would be missed; the employer would remain in business, and the public would receive uninterrupted service.
The sort of tribunal I have in mind would consist of three members who might be selected from a larger panel of persons who would be appointed by the government and who would have special training in law, economics and labour matters. A larger panel than three would be necessary to make sure that there would always be enough people available to form a tribunal and to take care of the possible need for more than one tribunal at certain times. These tribunals would, hopefully, weigh the arguments carefully and render a decision on the basis of what would be just and fair and in the public interest. What happens now is merely a test of strength as to which party can best withstand the punishment and hardship inflicted by a strike or lockout.
Labour has gained enormous strength and bargaining power throughout the years. Management groups are also very powerful. Management does, however, have certain checks which do not apply to labour. In most cases management has competitors, either domestic or foreign, or both, whom they must take into consideration. There are also laws against combines and price fixing. Nevertheless, there is a tendency for management to accept the demands of labour because they believe they can pass the increased costs involved on to the consumer. It is my opinion that this process has contributed greatly to rising price levels, to the inflation that threatens to price Canadian products out of the export market and which also tends to give foreign products an advantage in our own markets. Incidentally, this has recently become recognized by the federal government as our number one domestic problem. That is why I say that these tribunals should be able to keep the public interest as one of their prime considerations when dealing with disputes.
It may be argued by some that setting up machinery for compulsory arbitration would discourage meaningful negotiations, and result in a large number of disputes being referred to these tribunals. I doubt if this would happen. The very prospect that an arbitration award might go in favour of the other party, would be a powerful incentive for the disputants to make every effort to settle their differences themselves. Even if there were a large number of compulsory arbitrations at first, there might be compensa-21701-41J
Labour Tribunal Concerning Strikes tions, particularly if, as I would expect, the awards were made with the welfare of the country in mind.
The report of the Royal Commission on Labour Disputes in Ontario by the late former supreme court justice, Ivan C. Rand, recommended that the provincial government should have authority to designate essential industries where strikes would be prohibited, and would also forbid strikes by public employees. He also recommended that a provincial industrial tribunal be set up with wide powers to deal with labour-management disputes. I am suggesting in this motion that the federal government do likewise in areas of federal jurisdiction.
Mr. Justice Rand's recommendations produced a violent reaction from some labour spokesmen, as well as a certain amount of unfavourable comment from the management side. This, to my mind, bears out my contention that there would be enough apprehension about the results of arbitration by an impartial tribunal to prevent an undue rush to use such a service. The Woods Commission also recommended a three man public interest disputes commission, and I am going to quote from the same report again.
At page 170, paragraph 581, reads as follows:
We recommend that there be created a three man public interest disputes commission, independent of any government department, reporting to the Prime Minister, and composed of public members only. We recognize a potential difficulty in obtaining the consent of persons to serve on the public interest disputes commission, particularly if it were a full time responsibility. We therefore recommend that the commission be composed of persons serving part time, with a small full time secretariat of high calibre and with access to the Canada Department of Labour and other sources for assistance. To ensure that the members of the commission have the confidence of the parties as well as the public, the Canadian Industrial Relations Council, the creation of which we recommend later, should have the equivalent of tenure during overlapping terms of nine years each.
Paragraph 582 on page 171 reads as follows:
The commission would have two major functions. The first relates to determining special procedures for resolving industrial disputes in industries in the federal jurisdiction which, because of their record of industrial relations, are prone to disputes which are likely to jeopardize the public interest. The second function relates to the handling of actual disputes in any industry under federal jurisdiction where the public interest is threatened.
In fact, compulsory arbitration is quite common now in the field of labour relations, as well as in other fields such as damage
February 23, 1970
3978	COMMONS
Labour Tribunal Concerning Strikes suits, and compensation for expropriation of property. Labour grievances, matters of union jurisdiction, and alleged unfair labour practices, are subject to final adjudication by labour relations boards set up either by provincial governments or through collective agreements. It seems to me that the people who most fear the prospect of submitting to a fair and just settlement are those who have the most power to exact an unjustifiable one.
Sweden has been used as an example of a country with a fine record of industrial peace. Back in the 1920s and early 1930s that country was torn with the same sort of industrial strife that is plaguing our country today. When their labour court was first set up in 1928, it was strongly resisted by the unions. There were protest strikes and bitter charges that this court would be a tool of the employers. Gradually this instrument became accepted, and in fact the unions have made greater use of it than the industrialists. Sweden has had only three major strikes in the last 33 years.
Canada's population is about two and a half times that of Sweden, but in three recent years, 1964, 1965 and 1966, Canada lost more than nine million man days due to labour disputes, compared to 389,000 lost by Swedish workers, a ratio of 24 to 1, which means that our record for that period was about ten times worse than theirs.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Management-labour disputes have had a particularly detrimental effect this past year or two on the area I represent. Two strikes affected shipping on the Great Lakes for almost three months in 1968, damaging Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier of grain and other products, and quite probably losing us markets for our wheat which is currently in such large surplus. I would like to quote some editorial reaction to those strikes. This is taken from a T.V. editorial dated July 16, 1968:
The Seaway strike lasted 24 days and immobilized hundreds of ships in the Great Lakes ports and along the St. Lawrence. It meant a loss of at least $15 million to the ship owners. The Seaway Authority, the strikers, and sailors who were laid off because of it. So this is the immediate effect of the walk-out which to all the experts was considered a strike against essential service to the public. It is still too soon to evaluate the longterm consequences of this strike but we can foresee that there will be repercussions on our international trade in the months and years to come. It is clear that the Seaway and inland Canadian ports are no longer attractive to shipping, and that shippers intend to divert their cargoes to other ports. This attitude has been strengthened by the
[Mr. Douglas (Assiniboia) .1

fact that the labour problems in all the St. Lawrence ports leave much to be desired. We still ask the government the same question-what measures will be taken to prevent further work stoppages which affect the public interest and essential services?
Here is another editorial, from The Western Producer of September 16, 1968:
This is the kind of strike that should never have happened. There could be an endless argument as to how it was brought about-was the burden of the blame on one side or the other? The hapless bystander, the farmer, who suffers the greatest injury, hasn't enough information upon which to make a judgment. All he knows is that the union demanded a wage increase that would give its members parity with West Coast grain handlers, that the employers refused to meet these demands on the ground that they were prepared only to match increases in other local industries at the Lakehead and that both sides stuck to their inflexible positions until the Labour Minister moved in on them on Sunday, September 8.
Almost the same things could be said about the dispute which was recently settled at the west coast. In my opinion, we have lost sales and lost markets which we may never regain.
The thing the farmer is interested in, no matter where he places the blame, is that this kind of strike should not happen again. He does not wish to see the process of collective bargaining break down. He would, however, like to see some definite move made in the direction of establishing procedures for settlement if settlement cannot be reached through normal bargaining.
A strike of this kind is wrong, no matter where the blame is laid; it is wrong because of its damaging effect on grain farmers and other producers who depend on export sales, and on the whole economic structure of the country.
Then, there was the postal strike in 1968 which outraged people in every part of Canada, and there is the one that is hurting people in Montreal right now. The editor of the Rural Councillor, a publication of the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, had this to say in the September 1968 issue:
Sympathies vary between the workers and employers, depending on one's position. But, does anyone have sympathy for the innocent victims not responsible or involved in the disagreements, but who invariably suffer untold confusion in the management of their business, in addition to monetary loss? These people are hit hard by strikes, in which common sense, justice and reason are no longer the governing factors. Instead, supposedly intelligent people in our modern society revert to the ancient theory that "might is right". What a barbaric way to settle our economic problems!
Strikes are occurring one after the other like a plague on our society. It is high time our politicians faced this problem squarely and produced a solution based on justice-the same justice on which our whole way of life has developed over the years.
February 23, 1970

We have courts in our land for the sole purpose of administering justice, whether dealing with criminals or settling business and financial disputes. Let's outlaw strikes, and turn the labour squabbles over to courts conducted by experts, who have special knowledge in the social and economic life of our nation.
There is no system better devised by man, to deal with the processes of law, than our courts. This system will keep the nation's business moving without interruption, and labour and management can argue through the various courts of appeal with the assurance that in the end justice will prevail.
The Canadian public is looking to Parliament to take effective steps to reduce industrial strife significantly. As I stated earlier, this proposal is not aimed at the legitimate interests of either labour or management, but is rather to try to reach settlements based on justice and enlightened public interest.
The government has created an independent Prices and Incomes Commission to study, investigate and report on problems of rising costs and prices. The purpose of the commission is to discover the facts, analyse the root causes, processes and consequences of inflation, and to inform the public and the government on methods of achieving better performance in our economy. I hope that its influence will be such that all Canadians in positions of power are well informed as to the economic implications of their actions, and that they will exercise a greater degree of restraint in price and income determination, in their own long-term self-interest as well as that of the country as a whole.
I hope that government action along the lines recommended in this motion, coupled with the activities of an independent Prices and Incomes Commission, will result in a much better climate, conducive to the establishment of industrial peace in Canada, by substituting reason, good will and justice for what is far too often the law of the jungle. I hope other hon. members will support this motion.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO MAKE STRIKES ILLEGAL AND CREATE LABOUR TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, it would be very easy for me to support this motion proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) because it represents a possible, and in many ways practical, solution to one of the major ills facing our economy today which is, of course, the uncontrolled right to strike. I refer to the situation where a union concerns itself strictly with its own well being, strictly with the well being of its members, with no concern at all for the effect of the strike on the rest of society, with no concern at all for the impact it has on the nation's economy as a whole.
Labour Tribunal Concerning Strikes
Many times it has been pointed out how an employer, usually the large corporate entity, has in the past abused his power with respect to labour. This is generally acknowledged and has been true in some cases. Now, it is acknowledged in many quarters that the shoe is on the other foot, that labour has attained too much power and is wielding the big axe, abusing that power as it once accused employers of abusing it.
But in seeking solutions to these problems it is easy for us to look for direct and obvious measures, with no thought for the implications they may have in the future. Many people today advocate free enterprise for themselves, but controls and compulsion for someone else. Coming from an agricultural area I have sometimes seen this in certain sectors of agriculture, where people advocate controls and boards for other areas of the economy and free enterprise for themselves. If we were to propose compulsory controls for labour unions, we would be taking away a basic individual right of their members. We must look for a solution that will not infringe upon such a right.
I am no expert on labour relations but it seems to me we must always consider the fact that we cannot have compulsion in one area without having compulsion in another area. I believe it would be possible for the government, which has already done a little in this area, to establish price and wage guidelines. The government could say what it thinks wage increases could be, and what price increases could be, with the idea of relating them to productivity. Such guidelines could apply to businesses, the larger corporate entities, as well as to employees. In the case of employers, it would be possible for the government to control prices by means of tariff adjustments. I think we should reduce tariffs and regulate them. By importing goods from other countries we would keep prices in this area at a competitive and reasonable level. I think business in general would have to adjust to this competition.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
In the case of labour, I believe the same guidelines could apply. If labour did not conform to wage increase guidelines related to productivity, the government should see that the employers involved were protected in seeking alternate sources of labour. This would require a great many refinements. I realize this is rather a broad generalization, but I do not think we can allow labour to be
February 23, 1970
3980	COMMONS
Labour Tribunal Concerning Strikes as irresponsible in tying up the economy as it has been many times in the past.
The methods I have outlined of using tariffs to regulate business, of seeing that alternative labour sources could be used by business affected when the unions did not conform to the guidelines, would give to the unions and companies concerned the choice of conforming to government wage and price guidelines or else competing with imports or alternate labour sources. Whether or not the suggestions could be made workable, the fact remains that if voluntary controls cannot be effective, we may have no recourse but compulsory arbitration.
What we are experiencing in the realm of labour disputes is intolerable and devastating to our economy. I can cite no better example than that of the grain trade with which I am familiar and in which we have had many disputes over the years. These disputes always seem to come at key shipping times when it is critical to move grain. This has always been the time when unions have seen fit to make their demands. Consequently, we have ruined our reputation in the grain marketing area and have lost the sale of many millions of bushels. Our international reputation regarding wage disputes is poor. Often boats arriving in our ports have had to go awray empty or have been tied up for long periods costing a great deal of money in demurrage charges. This cannot go on. If there is no other recourse, I would be in favour of adopting the suggestion of the hon. member from Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas).

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO MAKE STRIKES ILLEGAL AND CREATE LABOUR TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any national industrial relations system reflects the character and temperament of its people, and sometimes the events surrounding the birth of the nation. It reflects also the national philosophy and, often, the dictates of the ruling or dominant class. The American revolution in the third quarter of the 18th century, with the constitutional guarantees that grew out of it-for due process of law, freedom of speech and assembly and against involuntary servitude- profoundly influenced the history and direction of labour relations and labour legislation in the United States. Sweden, for reasons of national economics and survival, has a system based on industry-wide bargaining. The
[Mr. Downey.)

United Kingdom has a system that is in its liberal, laissez-faire tradition, into which the labour government has tried to introduce legislative controls because of a faltering economy and serious balance of payment problems. The USSR has an authoritarian labour relations system in which the objectives of the state are paramount, a heritage of its own revolution.
In turning now more directly to the industrial relations system in Canada, it exemplifies what has been said above about the evolution simplicity to sophistication-though not as yet the more involved kind of sophistication to be found in some aspects of the industrial relations of the United States, though the two systems are basically similar.
The industrial relations history of Canada is marked by a number of significant influences. In the beginning, when industry became active, the earliest efforts toward union activity in Canada came in large measure from emigrant craftsmen from Great Britain. But unionism finds it hard to develop in a new country. The old country connection disappeared, to be replaced by the United States union ties that exist today in the vast majority of Canadian trade unions.
This American connection was deeply affected by the open border for labour which existed in the 19th century and for part of the 20th. There are persons still living who worked between Canada and the United States intermittently, and there are those who knew the Canadian and American printers and railwaymen who tramped or travelled freely between the two countries to take work as members of the same union and being assisted in finding work by their fellow unionists. Besides the early craft groups of printers, railwaymen and shoe workers, the Knights of Labour also came into Canada. Today we have some 108 international craft, multicraft and industrial unions in Canada.
It can be safely said that no Canadian has had more influence on the Canadian industrial relations system than Mr. Mackenzie King. His interest in labour was the basis of his fame, the foundation of his fortune, and the springboard to political office that made him Prime Minister of Canada for many years.
He was the genius behind present Canadian federal labour relations and disputes legislation which has roots going back to 1907, when it was the direct result of a bitter coal strike which took place during the previous winter in the coal fields of Alberta. The settlers of the province, living in tents and sod huts,
February 23, 1970

suffered great hardship and privation before the strike ended. Out of his experiences in attempting to settle this strike, Mr. Mackenzie King, then the deputy minister of labour, developed his famous labour philosophy that in any civilized community private rights must cease when they become public wrongs. In 1907, Parliament passed an act containing legislative principles designed to further this philosophy which have existed to this day, despite the enactment of successor legislation. The principles adopted were:
(1)	The public should not suffer from hasty or ill-considered strike or lockout action.
(2)	There should be no strike or lockout pending compulsory conciliation.
(3)	Public opinion, informed through the investigation and report of a board of conciliation, would exert an influence toward reasonableness in labour relations.
The second greatest influence on the Canadian industrial relations system was that arising from the United States New Deal legislation of the early 1930s. It will be recalled that following the crash of 1929, an economic depression enveloped the United States. When Franklin D. Roosevelt assumed the presidency in 1932, he initiated a number of extraordinary legislative measures in attempts to restore the shattered economy. One of these steps grew into the National Labour Relations Act, through which a trade union could compel an employer legally to engage in collective bargaining. It is beyond doubt that the growth of unionism, and particularly the development of the industrial form of union organization, were due to this beneficial representation and collective bargaining legislation.
This type of legislation spread to the Canadian provinces in the later years of the thirties and to the federal field of jurisdiction in 1944. It brought the same encouragement and growth of collective bargaining and trade unions as it had in the United States, by protecting the right to organize and to bargain collectively.
e (5:30 p.m.)
The influence of World War II on the Canadian industrial relations system and its participants was also very great. The co-operation of labour in producing war supplies and munitions in huge quantities was essential. This co-operation was obtained by further recognition and protection. A series of orders in council, passed pursuant to the War Measures Act, protected labour in the early years of the war prior to the wartime labour rela-

Labour Tribunal Concerning Strikes tions regulations, P.C. 1003, of 1944. The wartime labour relations regulations incorporated the representation and collective bargaining protection already mentioned as originating in the United States National Labor Relations Act. By the end of the war, organized labour had increased greatly in number, strength and status.
In 1948 the existing Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act was passed. It combined the dispute-settling provisions already mentioned as originating with Mr. Mackenzie King and the representation and collective bargaining provisions originating in the United States National Labor Relations Act.
As a result of all these events and circumstances, collective bargaining has emerged as the dominant influence and force in the industrial relations system in Canada. While only a third of the work force has been organized by trade unions, collective bargaining influences the wages and working conditions of a much greater proportion of industrial workers. Where conditions established by collective bargaining do not extend to unorganized workers, they are principally aided by labour standards legislation which provides minimum rates of wages, maximum hours of work, vacations with pay, statutory holidays, etc.
Collective bargaining is the keystone of the industrial relations system in Canada. Through it there is a very large measure of industrial self-determination of working conditions and wages, backed by the economic threat of strike by employees and lockout by employers. This institutional arrangement known as collective bargaining is relatively free in its functioning to the same extent as the other factors of production which determine interest, rent and profit. It is the indispensable element of a free, democratic society. It would be impossible to control or suppress collective bargaining without at the same time controlling other factors of production and destroying democratic institutions. Another dominant but less volatile feature of our industrial relations system is the vast amount of federal and provincial labour standards legislation which has been referred to already.
A third feature of our system is the widespread application of beneficial policy by Canadian governments apart from the provisions of direct labour legislation. For instance, there is the positive encouragement and promotion of good labour-management relations
February 23, 1970

Labour Tribunal Concerning Strikes as a matter of policy by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). This is done through the establishment of joint labour-management committees, the provision of preventive mediation, the provision of research facilities and the dissemination of information and statistics of value to labour and management in conducting their joint affairs.
Hon. members may wish to think about what system we might have in Canada if we did not have the prevailing industrial relations system. The alternatives to our present system of collective bargaining are basically two, or perhaps three. One alternative, unilateral decision-making by employers, has been challenged with increasing effectiveness by employees, their trade unions and governments since the first days of the industrial revolution. It is already impossible today as a way of industrial life, having been replaced by collective bargaining and by labour legislation designed to protect workers in various ways.
Another alternative is unilateral decisionmaking by the state, with legislation regulating all aspects of employment. This is not in our western democratic tradition, and from the viewpoint of production and productivity does not seem to be working out well in those eastern European countries where it has been tried. While we cannot attribute the benefits completely to collective bargaining, it is true that the western democratic countries that have given free rein to it have the highest productivity and the highest living standards in the world.
The third alternative that I mention as a possibility is a more enlightened form of collective bargaining on a tripartite basis, with labour and management having the active advice and assistance of governmental agencies in their bargaining relationship.
The current industrial unrest has brought all labour relations and disputes legislation under critical examination. This is also true with respect to the IRDI Act. In 1966 the then Prime Minister appointed a task force of academics of distinction to review the legislation and suggest revision. The task force made their report about a year ago and their recommendations are now under study. There will be some changes made in the legislation as a result, though not as many as are proposed.
The act as it now stands deals with four kinds of disputes:	(1) representation, (2)
unfair labour practices, (3) colllective agreement and (4) industrial grievances. Thirty-five


years ago federal legislation dealt only generally with disputes under one procedure, a conciliation board. There has been a procedural evolution since then whereby such disputes, other than collective agreement disputes, are submitted to processes of summary settlement by a Labour Relations Board, by arbitration or by court action. That is to say, decisive procedures have replaced strike or lockout action as the method of resolving representation, grievance and unfair labour practices disputes.
Existing legislation does not deal with controversies such as those arising suddenly because of displacement of workers by technological change. Five years ago the Freedman Commission made recommendations in this connection, and they also are being studied in connection with the revision of the federal act. It is reasonable to say now that sooner or later our industrial relations system will be radically altered because of the influence of automation, new methods, processes, techniques-all summed up as the technological revolution-in giving rise to disputes and special legislative measures for their settlement. The future of our industrial relations system, or parts of it, may be greatly affected. Canadians have to compete in an industrial world. Changes in our present industrial relations principles and legislation must not have an adverse impact on productivity and on our export trade. If this happens, labour and management, like the Swedes, may have to regulate themselves or be regulated in the national interest.
Industrial relations, collective bargaining, strikes and other phenomena are very much in the public eye today and, as I said earlier, it is difficult to find a person who is passive or neutral in such matters. A number of inquiries other than that of the federal task force have been sponsored by provincial governments and private agencies over the past few years, and most of them have been sparked by the high level of strike activity. These inquiries have sought to find out if we have in Canada adequate laws and policies for a stable industrial relations system and, where these are lacking, to recommend effective measures.
The adverse effects of technological change on employees and on collective bargaining have been a very live topic of study. Perhaps the most difficult question arising is whether we should continue to tinker with the present system or seek a new, bold and radical approach. Further, how can a new
February 23, 1970	COMMONS
approach succeed, living as we do in the shadow of the same system in the United States, with its closely connected business and trade union ties to Canada?
Whatever the system and its laws and policies, industrial disputes will always be with us. The methods of settlement will be different and will probably evolve in collective agreement disputes, as they have in the other types of disputes mentioned earlier, toward a more orderly method or procedure. Concerning the inevitability of disputes, it has been said, "Ever since Jacob went to work for his Uncle Laban and after seven years of toil received the wrong wife in payment, there have been disputes of one kind or another between employers of labour and those who work for them. Jacob, it will be recalled, protested bitterly against the injustice done him but his employer-uncle was a law unto himself and so Jacob had to make the best of it."

speechtext:
Last spring there were many ships waiting in the harbour at Vancouver. Many boxcars were scattered around the country; there were no locomotives to pull them. There was a great deal of No. 2 Northern to be hauled. The transportation system had broken down. Some hon. members would like to represent the situation as being different from what it was so as to provide an excuse for the motion we are now considering. I would point out that when this strike was on in Vancouver and when the ships were supposedly tied up, the SFU and the NFU-at that time they were separate-had an understanding that the grain would be handled. In spite of this, the hon. member for Assiniboia refers to unhappy and unfortunate events.
Mr. Speaker, the people of this country are well aware of the importance of free collective agreements. As time goes on and more people are affected by the economic ills of this period, they will realize even more clearly what negotiation and collective bargaining mean. The hon. member for Assiniboia is quite familiar with collective bargaining by the National Farmers' Union at the present time. The hon. member for Assiniboia appreciates, I realize, that the people generally must have representation. He knows the people realize that both management and labour are responsible. No one has suggested otherwise. We must also as a people decide whether what we are seeking is true collective bargaining or not. If our goal is industrial peace at any price, the way has been pinpointed by a number of countries including Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy a number of years ago. We know what was done by those countries which insisted on industrial peace at any price. People who refuse to subscribe to a policy of industrial peace at any price are surely not willing to endorse a policy of compulsion.
Let us consider the social implications of compulsory arbitration. The Dictionary of Sociology and Related Sciences suggests that arbitration is the process of referring disputes between employers and employees to a decision of impartial adjudicators whenever a collective labour
February 23, 1970
3984	COMMONS
Labour Tribunal Concerning Strikes agreement provides for the machinery of impartial adjudication. Compulsory arbitration, according to this dictionary, refers to a requirement that both parties submit their disputes to arbitration whether the collective agreement calls for it or not. The intent and definition of the word "compulsion" indicates a situation or process in which a person or group feels forced by external threat or danger to act against what had previously been in his or its interest and will or, alternatively, the act of compelling a reluctant person to perform acts against which the ego rebels.
It can readily be seen from this definition that compulsory arbitration is repugnant to our way of life in this country. The Minister of Labour should have a serious talk with his hon. friend from Assiniboia and tell him what his specialized industrial branch is all about. I am sure the hon. member would learn a great deal; the object is to beat out brush fires before they break into open flame threatening everything surrounding them. The desire for compulsion comes from political opportunists in a hurry to get somewhere, anxious to take up the cudgels because they believe the majority of people are not aware of the realities of the situation.
The hon. member suggested that this would be a temporary situation, one which would not last. But all of us, including the mover of this motion, should realize that to force unnecessary and undemocratic compulsory arbitration upon members of any society can result only in social demoralization or the loss of group morale, or the breakdown of personal habits, attitudes and social values through which individuals or groups of individuals maintain normal adjustment within society.

We have seen such a situation come about in many departments of government. We have heard ministers tell us what they intend to do to certain people. Mr. Speaker, you cannot talk to people in that way. There has to be meaningful negotiation, but it is not possible for there to be meaningful negotiation under the threat of compulsion. In order to bring about compulsory arbitration it is necessary to take away the rights and privileges of some of our people. The hon. member for Battle River expressed concern about work stoppages which affect every area of the country, but at the same time he realized that each individual is entitled to a fair share of the products of our society and


to an equal opportunity to express his wishes even if this means a little hardship at the time.
It is not hard to say we ought to pass legislation to take the place of collective bargaining. I would point out, however, that collective bargaining in Canada has a very good record. There have been instances, of course, when it has fallen down, with the result that other means have had to be found to take its place. Nevertheless, I believe the majority of the members of this House are reluctant to vote for bills calling an end to strikes.
In Saskatchewan we have experienced a situation in which the Premier of the province has crawled on the bandwagon, supposedly in the name of the people he claims to represent, and promises to call an election on the issue of work stoppages if he can. Mr. Speaker, the people of Saskatchewan are much better versed in these matters than they were in days gone by. I am confident that anyone who attempts to use a manoeuvre of this kind, either in this House or in the provincial legislature, will find his is a voice crying in the wilderness.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Labour-management disputes cannot be solved by means of compulsory arbitration. This cannot bring about increased peace on the labour front. Any member of this House who has had anything to do with the labour movement will appreciate that. What has been lacking is a really meaningful attempt by both labour and management to sit down and negotiate a true collective agreement. The government will not bring this about by passing legislation to provide for compulsory arbitration. The government cannot exercise compulsion in the sense of saying that unless the parties negotiate, compulsory arbitration will hand over their heads. I am sure no one here would like to see this state of affairs.
As I have said, compulsory arbitration brought about by the state will never succeed in replacing true collective bargaining. This is why I hope no member of the House will support the notice of motion that is before the House at this time. It seems to me that to do so would be an indication to the entire world that labour and management in this country are unable to look after their own affairs.
There are three items that must be considered, I suggest, in all collective bargaining processes. If these items had been considered hitherto, the hon. member for Assiniboia would not have felt impelled to introduce a
February 23, 1970	COMMONS
motion of this nature. I suggest that if prices, incomes and profits were taken into consideration in collective bargaining, no employee could justify an increase in his take-home pay unless prices had gone up. I am positive that every area of community life in this nation would be quite prepared to accept this proposition, and this is the way in which we will finally have to resolve our differences. It has been said that we should pass legislation to provide for the postponing of some labour disputes. I repeat that compulsion does not settle a dispute; all it does is postpone it.
I realize there are other hon. members who would like to say a few words before the vote comes at six o'clock, so in conclusion I contend that if we really mean what we say when talking of a free collective society, there is no place for compulsion whether it be in reaching collective agreement in this House of Commons or in any other sphere of Canadian life.

February 23, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill AFTER RECESS
The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner that Bill C-186, to establish a commission for the reform of the laws of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS AND DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to extend my congratulations to the government and, of course, to the minister for bringing in this long awaited and much needed piece of legislation. A reform of our laws is something which is long overdue. I only hope that this move on the part of the government will not prevent if from following through on something else which is badly needed and which I understand is under way at the present time, that is, a revision and consolidation of the laws of Canada. I understand this is presently being developed and it is something, of course, which will be welcomed by the members of the legal profession who have to refer quite often in the course of their practice to the statutes of Canada.
The purpose of this legislation, as I understand it, is to keep under review on a continuing basis the statutes of Canada. I was very happy to hear the minister say this afternoon that one of the items which would receive top priority was a revision of the Criminal Code of Canada. This is very necessary because there are many obsolete provisions in the Criminal Code which probably at one time served a useful purpose but which now have no place in our law. I made a hurried review of the code this afternoon and found Section 72, for example, which states:
Every one who
(a) challenges or attempts by any means to provoke another person to fight a duel... is guilty of an indictable offence-
That provision, of course, is no longer necessary under Canadian law. I do not think too many duels are fought at the present time.
Section 179(h) provides that no person shall for valuable consideration carry on or


play or offer to carry on or play, or employ any person to carry on or play in a public place or a place to which the public has access the game of three-card monte. I wonder how often three-card monte is played in modern society. These laws, of course, were probably necessary at the time the code was originally drafted.
Then we have section 308 which provides:
Every one who fraudulently
(a) pretends to exercise or to use any kind of witchcraft... is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
I do not think there is much witchcraft practised in Canada today; at least, I hope there is not.

These are some of the anachronisms which are presently contained in our Criminal Code and which only take up valuable space. They should be deleted. For that reason I was particularly happy to hear the minister say that one of the first things which would be considered by this law reform commission would be the Criminal Code, with a view to revising it Where necessary after taking a close look at it.
For the most part this is a good bill. There are some provisions to which I think some objection can be taken. One of the things which bothers me particularly is the tremendous power vested by this bill in the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). I have every confidence in the present Minister of Justice, but there will come a time when he will no longer occupy that position. If we pass the statute in its present form, we will be giving very great powers to people of whom we have no conception.
The bill provides that every appointee to the law reform commission must first have the approval of the minister. In other words, no man can be appointed to this commission unless he has the approval of the minister. Clause 3 of the bill provides:
A commission is hereby established to be known as the Law Reform Commission of Canada, consisting of a chairman, a vice-chairman, two other full-time members and two part-time members to be appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the minister.
So the minister actually is the man who will say who shall comprise this commission. Under clause 7(2) the minister will decide what remuneration shall be paid to part-time members. In other words, he will say what money the part-time members will
February 23, 1970	COMMONS
receive for their services. I suppose the minister will naturally be anxious to have people as competent as possible appointed to the commission, but I think this provision gives him a little too much power when it suggests that he in his own discretion shall decide how much money these people are to be paid.
Let me refer to clause 12 of the bill which provides:
In carrying out its objects, the commission (a) may receive and consider any proposals for the reform of the law-
It does not have to receive them, but it may receive them. Then it goes on to state that the commission-
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
-shall, in accordance with any programs for studies described in paragraph (c) that are approved by the minister, undertake or direct the undertaking of studies-
In other words the minister, not the commission, shall decide what studies are to be undertaken. Further, it states that the commission-
-shall, with the concurrence of the minister and to the extent that the commission is able to do so without, in its opinion, impairing its ability to carry out any studies that have been or are to be undertaken by it pursuant to paragraph (d), provide information, research material and study results and make recommendations to departments-
In other words, only with the concurrence of the minister can the law reform commission do these things. Then we find this provision:
The commission shall include in any program for studies prepared by it pursuant to paragraph (c) of subsection (1) any study requested by the minister-
The only study it can undertaken is one requested by the minister. Then it states:
-and the commission shall, in determining its priorities for studies in relation to any such programs, be governed by any request so made to it.
Therefore, the commission must be governed, not by its own feelings or its own discretion but rather by what the minister says. Clause 13 states:
The commission may in its discretion and with the concurrence of the minister undertake any particular study-
As I see it, the whole thing depends on what the minister says. This commission is to be composed of six or seven men, at least five of whom must be either judges or barristers of at least ten years' standing in the profession. Surely, if we are to have a commission

Law Reform Commission Bill made up of such qualified men as these we should be able to leave to their discretion what they should undertake and what recommendations they should make, rather than have them under the direct control of the minister. I submit that the bill leaves too much discretion in the minister and not enough in the commission itself, which of course would be composed of very eminent and highly qualified people.
The bill provides, further, that the commission may receive and consider any proposals for the reform of the law. I only hope the commission will try to do this as closely as possible to its base. One thing that has astounded me is the tremendous amount of money involved in sending committees and commissions all over this country to study problems which in many instances could be studied just as carefully here in Ottawa.
I took the time to look up the record. I find that last year the Agricultural Committee in its eastern and western tours cost this country $65,711.88. The Committee on Transport and Communications visited Charlottetown, which is not very far away. That trip cost the taxpayers of this country $18,244.35. The Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts travelled only to Montreal. That trip cost $3,796.87. Last year the External Affairs Committee went overseas to visit the NATO bases. That trip cost $19,093. Then it went to Halifax, at a cost of $1,150. The Committee on Fisheries and Forestry last year travelled to the west coast. By the way, I was a member of the committee and took part in that trip. The cost involved was $53,295.29.

I believe it would be much cheaper to bring witnesses to Ottawa than to have committees travel all over Canada. Although this commission, naturally, will have to inquire into many aspects of the law or reform of the law and

our experience in committees is that the government and the minister seem very reluctant to make any changes to a bill as originally drafted. Those of us who have served on committees must be impressed by that fact: no matter how strong or logical an argument one puts forth, it seems almost impossible to convince the powers that be that some changes could satisfactorily be made to the bill as drafted. I do not know why this should be.
Actually, this is what we have committees for-to study bills in every detail, to make recommendations to the minister and subsequently to report to the House. So while I do not have very much hope that many changes will be made to this bill at the committee stage, I suggest very seriously to the minister that he give consideration to some of the changes which I feel would make the bill more workable and which would incite the committee to do a better job.
After all, if you are going to appoint a committee of competent men, you must have confidence in them; and if they are going to do a good job, they must feel they have some leeway in their work. As I read the bill, the law reform commission will not have too much leeway. All it will be able to do is make recommendations which then must be approved by the minister.
The minister pointed out this afternoon- this is a good feature of the bill so far as it goes-that he is required to report to the House on the work of the commission. But I call the attention of the House to clause 18 of the bill which states that the minister shall, within 15 days after the approval by him of each program of studies, make his report to the House. He does not necessarily have to make a report to the House of every program of studies recommended by the commission, but only of programs of study which have first been approved by him.
Why should he not be required to report to the House on all the programs of studies which have been recommended by the commission? He is the one who decides which programs shall be submitted to the House. A very worth-while program of studies, at least in the opinion of the commission, may be submitted to the minister but he only reports to the House on those which have first been approved by him.
These are some of the things which I feel have a tendency to destroy our democratic system of government. I do not care how confident a minister is, after all, he is only a human being and he has all the failures of a
February 23, 1970	COMMONS
human being. I feel it is wrong to put too much power in the hands of any one man. I am afraid this is what the bill does. As I said, it has many good features and this type of legislation is long overdue. However, I hope the minister will give serious consideration in committee to making changes along the line of some of the recommendations which have been made during the second reading stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a full review of the Criminal Code is long overdue and I am pleased that Bill C-186 envisages reforms on a very wide range of subjects. If the House will bear with me for a few minutes, I would like to outline a few areas requiring reform which have come to my attention, especially during my career as a law enforcement officer.
I agree with previous speakers who have expressed the hope that having set down that the chairman and vice-chairman of the commission must be chosen from among judges or notable members of the Bar, this commission would be better balanced by ensuring that some of the appointees come from branches of society which have to deal with the law from the people's point of view, or at least from the point of view of people who have had to administer the law at the grass roots level. I say this because there is no branch of public life wherein greater harm can be done than when law is divorced from common sense.
So right from the start I hope-because the duration of the appointment of these people might be for as long as seven years-that great care will be taken to appoint men who have experience in the humanities. I will not make any suggestion beyond that. I think that all those within sound of my voice know perfectly well what I mean.
I am alarmed at the sweeping powers given in this bill to a minister of the Crown. I do not know that this is necessary, particularly in view of the fact that our House of Commons is being subdivided into committees of specialists. I would like to see whether the committees system will really blossom into full flower and produce the results which I know it can produce if given the power. Committees should have a great deal to do in seeing that the intentions of Parliament, when we put something into statute form, are carried out.
I for one do not know any one person to whom I would be willing to delegate full and supreme authority in such an important matter as law enforcement throughout the
DEBATES	3989
Law Reform Commission Bill country. It has worked reasonably well in the past perhaps, but with the high incidence of well-organized crime-I might say even international crime-we have to ensure that every safeguard is taken to give a fair and just hearing to everyone.
It appears to me that there is a danger when a minister of the Crown is given such tremendous authority, not only in issuing his flats for the prosecution but in withholding them. If any lawyer in Canada wishes to look them up, he can read the record of notable cases where the file has not been used when it should have been used. Unfortunately, we can also say that in the hands of unscrupulous men the power to put out the long arm of the law to padlock people out of their rightful places of assembly or of business has been abused.
It is not always possible for the little people, particularly, to go to the higher courts of the land to obtain justice. I have every respect for our Supreme Court of Canada, but one can get to that august body only if one can afford the tremendous costs involved and has the time for the long delays necessary to get there. I have read some of the judgments, to which I take off my hat and which I respect; but it is a long and hard road for the small man with limited means to get to that high court. Perhaps this subject is not too wide in scope and is within the terms of the statute and the powers we will give the commission to enable it to look into this and related matters.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
In fact, as I see it the terms of reference contained in this legislation and the powers of the commission should be such-with the few exceptions mentioned by the previous speaker-that the whole gamut of Canadian law can be reviewed. I apply the same caveat to this subject; that where there are abuses, I do not think it should be left in the hands of any one minister of the Crown to say what subjects are to be reviewed or even what priorities are to be assigned to them.
We have within Parliament a fully capable justice committee. We have plenty of jurists to serve on it, with a total of hundreds of years of experience at the Bar. They are quite competent to report to Parliament and to work in liaison with the executive arm of government and this commission which, as I say, I hope will make a full investigation into every branch of our law.
February 23, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill
There are certain things which I hope the commission will look into very carefully. Whether you attack the problem from the point of view of the lawyer who is defending or the lawyer who is prosecuting, from the point of view of the lesser officials of the court, or whether you are one of the principals in an action, you must be impressed- although sometimes dismayed-by the archaic laws of evidence which we have to assist the courts in bringing justice to everybody concerned. All too often these laws of evidence, which are supposed to protect the innocent and give redress to those who are wronged, tend to shelve the whole problem-sometimes to protect those who are most guilty and to give little redress to those who need it.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), who is an experienced man in these matters, touched upon the law of insanity which in its present form is far from adequate. With up-to-date psychiatrists, psychologists and criminologists working together it should be possible to devise something better than the M'Naghten rules so that people will not be able to hide behind faked insanity.
The question of bail has been brought forcefully to my attention on various occasions. Recently the law on bail has been improved, but it is still very difficult for a young lad with no means and of no fixed abode to escape the first inequity of the law. If he has no family, no money and nobody to speak for him, he may languish in jail for a considerable time. At the end of that time, whether innocent or guilty, he has been behind bars-and that is not a good place to be. I venture to say that with our modern methods of keeping track of people and the great stake our young people have in their own security, most young men are hardly likely to leave the country. Bail, after all, is just a guarantee to the court that the living body of John Doe will appear to answer the charge laid against him.
Many young people who are without support are away from home trying to establish a home of their own. They do not have the physical resources, in terms of money, to return home. I speak from experience when I say it is all too easy to round up all the loose lads in town under the pretext that you think they have committed a crime. It is a serious matter to these young boys and to society as a whole. A young offender-and he is not always an offender; he may be just a suspect-occasionally has his future course of


action dictated by his first contact with the law. That first contact often sets the path for him-whether he returns to be a productive member of society or whether he sets off on the road to crime.
In fact, if a young boy is innocent and is badly treated during that first contact with the law, he may very well turn to a life of crime. If a young man has been under arrest for three or four weeks in a new community, and everybody knows about it, it is difficult for him to convince the public that he has been held without bail though innocent of any offence.
I hope the commission will also be rapidly seized with the problem of seeing what can be done to standardize many of our quasi criminal statutes, such as our traffic laws and liquor laws, which stipulate certain criminal offences of which we are all guilty from time to time. There is no uniformity in these laws across Canada. You would have to be a Philadelphia lawyer to know what your rights are when you take a drink or park your car in every jurisdiction in Canada. Surely it is not beyond the powers of the federal and provincial ministers of justice to devise some kind of consensus on what normal standards of Canadian behaviour should be in this regard. I hope the commission will feel free to recommend, if necessary, changes in our constitution which will make this possible. If it is impossible for provincial officials to give up their power to the federal authority in this respect, and vice versa, surely this is a question concerning the good of Canada; therefore, I hope the commission will quickly be seized of that problem.
A great effort should be made to standardize penalties across Canada. There is a ridiculous spread between what happens to various law offenders in this country. You will hear of a case, perhaps in British Columbia, where a boy goes to jail for six months for stealing a packet of cigarettes. In another place he will get a suspended sentence. If you are languishing in jail for six months, and you know of a friend of yours who got a suspended sentence for the same offence in another jurisdiction, it is quite natural for you to feel badly treated. The fact that a person knows what the penalty will be under the law can be a deterrent of itself in a great many cases. It is an assurance that a person knows how he will be treated. And if we achieve uniformity in penalties, a great deal more can be done between magistrates and judges to work out some kind of uniformity in the treatment of offenders.
February 23. 1970

People are sometimes more careful when penalties are spelled out in the statutes. Now there is no escape when one is found guilty on a charge of drunken driving. As already noted by Canadian law enforcement officers, the very fear of being nabbed by the breathalyzer has had a considerable effect on the driving public. They are afraid of a scientific test. A breathalyzer reading of .08, whether it is a fair level or not, is a scientific measurement; and when a driver knows he is near .08 he becomes quite concerned about getting into jeopardy with the law.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I think a great deal can be done if this commission will get together with the attorneys general and other law enforcement people in the provinces to work out standard methods. As every lawyer knows, there are different rules of procedure in every province of Canada. If they were standardized, a lawyer who takes his training in Ontario, say, would feel at home practising in any other province. It may be that some of these rules have been handed down from the old family compacts, the monopolies of ancient times, but many of these old monopolies and outworn procedures are going by the board today. This is one field in which I think a revamping of our whole attitude to public service should be gone into very thoroughly.
It would be very helpful-though perhaps this is asking too much-if the commission could take our courts and the appointment of judges out of day-by-day politics. I have often said that I do not like to see Crown corporations created, though they are above politics, and I know the people who recommend them are just trying to do what I am recommending now, that is, they are trying to elevate certain areas of our public service out of the realm of dirty politics.
Though the appointment of judges has been very fair in the past, it is an area that might well be looked at. While they are at it, the commission might look into the circumstances when a judge is suspected of violating the very high standards of behaviour expected of him in public life. We had an example of this a few years ago when it was deemed necessary to bring a judge before a parliamentary committee. Whether that particular judge asked to come before the committee is irrelevant, is history. I know I was shocked at the time, and sometimes the methods used appear to be those of the Star Chamber. This commission might look into the question of how judges are to be disciplined if necessary. There must

Law Reform Commission Bill be a better method of removing a judge than treating him as though he were guilty of a traffic offence.
There is, and should be, a standard of the highest order for appointees to the bench; but there should be no hiatus in the law when stern action is required to ensure the maintenance of those high standards. Judges should know the terms of their appointment and should know also, should the occasion arise, what sort of tribunal will be seized with the responsibility of determining whether they are fit to continue to serve in that capacity.
They should also know, of course, whether they have earned any part of their retirement allowance. In this day and age their security is as inviolable as anybody else's and the terms of their appointment should be clearly set out. Let us not be inverted snobs and say that a poor man has rights but a judge has not: he has the same rights in the tribunals of Canada, from the magistrate's court to the Supreme Court, as anyone else. I do not think the case to which I have referred was handled in a very dignified manner and consequently I should like this question to be one of the terms of reference of the commission.
I am not happy that the personnel of this board should be restricted necessarily to judges and lawyers in the strict sense that they must be on the bench or barristers. If we could get men of international renown such as the great international lawyer Freidman who sat at the Nuremburg trials, they should not have to qualify as a member of the Bar of Canada. Then there is Mr. Finkelman, who has made a great contribution to labour law and who knows the law from the grass roots, from the mines to the lumber camps and the lower echelons of labour in the country. This is the type of man who knows how a criminal code or labour code will work amongst the masses.
When this bill goes to committee, as I presume it will, for further study I hope this aspect of the matter will be looked into very carefully. I think it is a little restrictive in this respect and I am sure it is within the prerogative of the minister, in the final decision, to accept men such as the two I have mentioned who may not necessarily have practised at the bar but who perhaps have as great a knowledge of jurisprudence and the interpretation of statutes as anybody in the country. Very often it is in the misinterpretation of statutes that injustice occurs. The intention of Parliament is often frustrated because statutes have not been properly

Law Reform Commission Bill foamed. Therefore, it is important that the men appointed to this commission be very well-balanced men who are not only conversant with the law as written but as it is interpreted and practised.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the Interpretation Act, which governs all the statutes of Canada, might be thoroughly gone over at the same time. There are occasions when a witness is given the protection of the Canada Evidence Act, and this act should also be overhauled. We do not want mere words to frustrate the intention of the Criminal Code of Canada. As we all know, there is a danger in codifying a law as it is then liable to lose an element of common sense. The written word is often taken as the true spirit of the law, so it is most important that the right people are put in the position of framing laws. It is practically impossible to interpret a stupid law, so it is of utmost importance that the law be properly framed in the first place.
I would be satisfied with the type of law which they have in England, the English common law. If we codify it and say on paper what the statutes are, we will cut down the human error of judges. We must be very careful about what is put on paper. It must be wisely done, clear and practically beyond argument, if that is possible. The responsibility upon this commission and upon the men who are to oversee it is of the highest order.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: EXEMPTION OF CERTAIN PRACTICES FROM PROVISIONS OF COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-184, to exempt certain shipping conference practices from the provisions of the Combines Investigation act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the over-all objective of this bill is to exempt certain of the practices of steamship conferences from the operations of anti-combines legislation and to attach conditions to the granting of the exemption. This bill really results from the report of June 17, 1965, of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission in which it was found that certain practices of shipping conferences contravened the Combines Investigation Act.
Characteristic features of this breach are that conferences-if hon. members are not familiar with that term, they are associations of shipping lines serving precisely-defined general cargo ocean trades-by formal agreement between their members adhere to common tariffs of rates and charges and, typically, to restrict competition, bind shippers to use only conference line vessels by a form of contract known as an exclusive patronage contract, or shippers rate agreement, in which the inducement to the contract signatory is that he will have applied to his shipments a schedule of rates which is lower than that applied to non-contract signatories.
There are other more innocuous practices, and yet others which the commission found objectionable in any circumstances. The Restrictive Trade Practices Commission none the less concluded that as an alternative to unbridled competition characterized by fluctuating rates and irregular service, conferences perform a useful and desirable function by providing a stable rate structure and regular and frequent service, and that the performance of this function was generally accepted by
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act Canadian exporters and importers as reasonably satisfactory. Accordingly, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission recommended that in certain respects, and subject to certain safeguards, shipping conferences be exempted from the application of the Combines Investigation Act. The alternative possibility was proceedings under the act to secure a prohibition order, but for the broad reasons cited the commission did not recommend such proceedings.
The report of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission and its recommendations were subjected to detailed and lengthy study by an interdepartmental committee which in due course in its report substantially approved the recommendations. In December, 1968, the then Minister of Transport, with the concurrence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, devised a series of recommendations. This bill really implements those recommendations.
By nature, the bill is primarily a transport and trade measure with implications in the field of external relations. It is directed toward the protection of those Canadians who are users of ocean transport which means, directly or indirectly, substantially all Canadians. It substitutes regulation and scrutiny while safeguarding a degree of competition as an alternative to the unrestricted competition that would result from the application of the Combines Investigation Act. The legislation will extend only to international shipping. Shipping between Canadian ports is not exempted and will continue to be subject to the Combines Investigation Act and other applicable statutes.
It will be seen that by clause 11 the power of the director to make inquiries in the field of transportation is expanded. The bill is not unique, incidentally, in permitting a degree of collaboration between carriers. Section 337 of the Railway Act, as amended by section 53 of the National Transportation Act, reads as follows:
337. Railway companies shall exchange such information with respect to costs as may be required under this act and may agree upon and charge common rates under and in accordance with regulations or orders made by the commission.
An important point to be noted is that conferences have been in existence since the latter part of the nineteenth century; that is to say, their development more or less coin-
February 23, 1970
3998	COMMONS
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act cided with the development of regular steamship liner services after the end of the era of sail.
The value of the conference function has been acknowledged by governments throughout the world, sometimes with tacit approval and sometimes reluctantly. Subsequently, all governments have been obliged to permit the operation of conferences because no suitable alternative mechanism to provide stability and service has been developed. For example, the government of the United States, by the Shipping Act of 1916, explicitly exempted conferences from the Sherman anti-trust laws, but by the same act applied extensive and detailed regulations. The U.S.A. position was confirmed by an amendment to the Shipping Act in 1961, which in part clarified the law and in part strengthened and increased the degree of regulation.
However, hon. members may be aware that a conference is necessarily composed of shipping lines, but a shipping line is not necessarily a conference member and, indeed, many shipping lines operate independently, frequently in competition with conferences. It might be useful if I attempted to define what is a shipping line. To begin with, a shipping line is not necessarily a corporate entity by itself. Many shipping companies operate several so-called lines.
The essential characteristic of a shipping line is that it performs a scheduled and advertised common carrier service from named ports to named ports. This is very different from the type of service performed by so-called tramp vessels which, generally speaking, are chartered to carry full cargoes anywhere in the world as inducement offers. Liners and tramps tend to be somewhat different in design, but they need not be so and, indeed, liner operators have traditionally chartered tramps to augment their liner fleets in times of high demand. The real difference is in the type of service. I re-emphasize that the shipping line is one that operates between named ports.
