This bill has no application to the tramp trades. The question whether or not there is, or should be, a Canadian merchant marine is not relevant to this bill. Canadian flag ocean-going ships would operate either in the liner trades or the tramp


trades, and the owners of those in the liner trades would decide to become conference members or operate independently for commercial reasons that would not be different from those of owners of other nationalities.
This bill has the same application to all conference members, regardless of their nationality and of the flags flown by their vessels. Violations under this bill are in two categories which might be described as major and minor. Major violations are those which impose the application of the Combines Investigation Act and will arise from certain breaches of clauses 3 and 4 of the bill. Minor violations are failure to file certain documents as required by clauses 5, 6 and 7. The penalty, to be found in clause 8, is a fine of $100 a day which in practice is likely to apply to every member of a conference that is in breach.
The filing requirements are important in that they expose the basic conference relationships to public scrutiny. Thus, the bill accomplishes the dual purpose of providing conditional exemption and enabling continuous scrutiny. The bill covers all important aspects of the contractual relationships between members of a conference on the one hand and between the conference and shippers on the other, and is a recognition on the part of the government of its duty to protect the interests of its citizens.
Indeed, it might well be said that under the national transportation policy as enunciated in the National Transportation Act there is a duty to seriously scrutinize and seek to influence ocean shipping upon which Canadians are so enormously dependent. Perhaps not the least important aspect of this duty is the responsibility imposed on the Canadian Transport Commission by section 14 of the National Transportation Act to perform its function "with the object of co-ordinating and harmonizing the operations of all carriers engaged in transport."
This is in some respects a rather complex measure and I have no doubt that at the committee stage members will wish to examine its various clauses in detail. Of course, there will be expert witnesses in this rather complicated area in order to attempt to answer questions of members. I believe I have in these few remarks, however, set the scene and explained why we feel it is necessary to bring forth this legislation at this time.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the minister for bringing in this measure based on the recommendation of the Combines Investigation Branch, because it only recognizes what has been going on for a long time anyway and what is inevitable in this field. It is making an honest woman out of the minister's non-tramps. It is legitimizing something that is going on.
What I like about this legislation is that at least it is honest and above board and we can see what is going on. There is nothing worse in this country than pretending we have competition in some areas when in fact it does not exist. This has been the case with shipping of this kind for a long time. I suggest that we could benefit substantially by expanding this principle to other sectors of our economy. There are many areas of our economy in which there is supposed to be unbridled competition, when in fact there is no competition and instead what you have is price leadership.
In that situation the strong in the industry permit some of their weaker competitors to

DEBATES	February 23, 1970
limp so that the stronger can take higher profits. If you try to look at their operations they say they have lots of competition, when in fact it does not exist. It is for this reason that I prefer to see things above board. In a case of this kind, when we recognize that there is an agreement, where there is collusion among the shippers, if they abuse this privilege and the rates are raised too much somebody will step in and they will be watched. We know what the situation is in this industry now.
When we had a similar example we had to step in and remove some of the competition, which was becoming very destructive in the case of the west coast fishermen, because it simply did not make any sense. There is only enough business for a certain number of people to earn a livelihood. If too many get in, instead of reducing costs it simply raises them-no one can make a living because of the unbridled competition and the senseless anarchy that prevails in such a situation.
One of the difficulties we face in this country is that we have inherited a pattern of competition from the United States that does not really make any sense for Canada. If you look back at the history of the combines legislation you will see that Canada brought in the legislation at just about the same time as did the United States. In the United States, a country eleven times our size, a case can be made for much more competition than in a country such as Canada.
Where you inherit the U.S. form of competition, where you have, as we have here, the number of branch plants which are almost a Dinky toy replica of U.S. companies, you wind up with a terribly inefficient structure in your industry and economy. If you examine our economy you will find that almost everywhere that U.S. branch plants have moved in, the effectiveness and competitiveness of Canadian industry has been destroyed. Contrary to much of the conventional wisdom that is held forth in this country about the great advantage of U.S. investment in Canada, I think it has destroyed our ability to be efficient and competitive and in the long run will lower our standard of living rather than raise it.
It may be true that when capital first came in, we got off a little faster; we got a better start than we might have otherwise. But in

fact, if you watch these industries develop you will find that the first advantage disappeared very quickly. It is interesting to note that perhaps the most efficient industries that exist in this country are either privately or publicly-owned industries in Canadian hands-such as the steel industry, which remains largely in Canadian hands-Crown corporations and the beer industry. I could go on in this way.
My comments will not be very extensive. The point I am trying to make in supporting this legislation is that it is realistic; that we are facing up to certain facts. Mr. Speaker, almost a month ago I raised the point that housewives across the country, through the daily use of detergents are forced to contribute heavily and unwillingly to water pollution in Canada, and I asked if the government was considering asking the National Research Council to initiate an emergency research program to develop a non-phosphate, non-pollutive detergent. That was on January 28, nearly a month ago. A lot of water has gone under the bridge and over the dam since then-and a great deal of it polluted.
The situation has now changed because in the meantime we have had full details of a non-phosphate detergent which exists, which has been tried out and which has been given very wide publicity. In fact, I believe the program "W5" last night was seen by people from coast to coast and the result will probably be that in addition to the 500 letters I received in my office during the last week, I will receive another inundation of mail this week on the same subject. My consolation is to know that a great many members on the government side of the House are also receiving a flood of the same type of mail. I am glad that consumers are concerned enough to send this mail to us.

February 23, 1970

Dr. Philip Jones of the University of Toronto has now given us details of Formula N, which to the best of my knowledge is the only non-phosphate detergent in existence. Sweden has a detergent of this type, but it has 8 per cent phosphate content in it. Formula N is absolutely phosphate free and is non-polluting. Further, it cleans as well as the phosphate kind, and in many kinds of washing cleans better. It has been tried out by a group of Toronto housewives over a period of three months. I believe it was also tried out expri-mentally on Saturday last by a number of people in a laundromat, with the same result. In the third place, it takes only half as much detergent as the regular phosphate type to do a wash. In the fourth place, according to Dr. Jones it can be manufactured much more cheaply.
The present problem is not for the Research Council to initiate an emergency program to find a non-phosphate, non-polluting detergent, because we have it. As Dr. Jones has made clear, research must be kept up and this product improved, if possible, by continued research. There are two steps which should be taken by the government now. First of all, detergents containing phosphates should be banned at the earliest possible moment. The minister has said that he will aim for a complete ban by 1972 and will phase it out in several stages, that he will make amendments to the Canada Water Act in this direction, and that he now has the agreement of the provinces to proceed with an amendment to the Criminal Code.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I should like to see this timetable speeded up. The phasing-out could be achieved more quickly, now that there is an alternative available. Banning detergents containing phosphates is the first thing. The second is the government's responsibility to get Formula N on the market as quickly as possible in order to avoid a serious cause of pollution.
We have Crown corporations to handle a great many things that private enterprise cannot handle adequately. We have had great success with Polymer. In this House we set up a fresh fish marketing corporation, the uranium corporation, and there is Devco which has made a success of the steel industry in Sydney. If the detergent companies are too slow about getting this new non-phosphate
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion detergent onto the market, I cannot see why the government should not set up a Crown corporation to make it available to concerned consumers across the country. If other companies come along later, then the government is already providing healthy competition to try and save our waterways.
There should be an immediate regulation to enforce upon manufacturers the need for listing the phosphate content on existing detergent packages. "Pollution Probe" and "STOP" have done a wonderful job in publishing the phosphate content of detergents presently on the market, but I do not think that should keep the government from its responsibility of insisting that the contents be listed on detergent packages or other containers for cleansing agents. The consumers of this country are not fooling about wanting to see phosphate detergents wiped out. They are tremendously concerned and worried about the damage occurring daily to our streams and waterways.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I urge that these steps be taken with the least possible delay: first of all, the banning of detergents; second, getting this new non-phosphate detergent on the market; and third, pending that, requiring manufacturers to list phosphate content on detergent packages and containers.

It does not

We have the problem of what we should do about phosphates. I defy anyone in this House or anywhere else to say that when phosphates were first introduced in detergents they had any idea of what would happen. The problem is to rid ourselves of phosphates in the detergents of this country. We must ensure that whatever kind of replacement there is-and we still have to wash our clothes and clean our dishes-it will not have an effect on our waterways, as the hon. lady said, so that in four, five or ten
years from now we do not have the same kind of situation that we now have.
I commend the hon. lady for her comments. I know what she means. 1 know the Canadian people are concerned. I believe that we must place the responsibility on the shoulders of the people who have the major investment in this industry, the detergent manufacturers. We say to them: This is what must happen: you must reduce the amount of phosphates; you must find a replacement. It is up to the private sector to come up with their own ideas. Perhaps the government can help through the National Research Council or other agencies, but I believe it is up to the private sector to make the first move.
